meta.blurb: Shere Khan the tiger wants the human baby that crawled into the wolves' cave, but Mother Wolf will not give him up. The boy, Mowgli, grows up with a bear and a panther as teachers. The tiger is patient.
meta.bible: Mowgli: the man-cub, called the Frog, raised by wolves in the Seeonee hills of India. Father Wolf and Mother Wolf: the wolves who take Mowgli in; they have four cubs. Akela: the old grey leader of the Seeonee Pack. Gray Brother: the eldest of Mother Wolf's cubs and Mowgli's faithful friend. Shere Khan: the great tiger, lame from birth, who hunts Mowgli and fears fire. Tabaqui: the sly jackal who carries tales. Baloo: the sleepy old brown bear who teaches the Law of the Jungle. Bagheera: the sleek black panther who buys Mowgli's place in the Pack with a bull. Kaa: the huge rock python who helps against the monkeys and does the Dance of Hunger. Bandar-log: the Monkey People, who have no Law, no leader and no memory. Chil: the kite, a bird who carries the news. Cold Lairs: the ruined city where the monkeys take Mowgli. Council Rock: the flat rock where the Pack meets. Red Flower: the jungle's name for fire. Law of the Jungle: the rules every jungle animal keeps. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: a young mongoose, washed out by a flood, adopted by an English family in India. Teddy: the family's small son; his father and mother live in the bungalow. Darzee: a brave tailorbird who lives in the garden. Nag: a great black cobra. Nagaina: his wife. Their eggs are hidden in the melon bed. Kala Nag: the old working elephant, Black Snake. Little Toomai: a ten-year-old boy whose father and family drive elephants; he sees the elephants dance and is named Toomai of the Elephants. Messua: the kind village woman whose small son was carried off long ago by a tiger. Rama: the great bull who leads the village buffaloes. Lungri: the Lame One, the wolves' name for Shere Khan. Master-Words: the Jungle's password, "We be of one blood, ye and I". Oodeypore: the city where Bagheera was born in a king's cage. Karait: a small, dusty brown, deadly snake. Chuchundra: the timid muskrat who creeps along the walls. Big Toomai: Little Toomai's father, Kala Nag's driver. Pudmini: a she-elephant of the camp. Petersen Sahib: the white officer in charge of catching elephants. Machua Appa: the chief of the drivers. Keddah: the great wooden stockade where wild elephants are driven. Buldeo: the boastful old hunter of the village. Nathoo: Messua's lost son. The story keeps to the order of Kipling's tales: Mowgli's Brothers, Kaa's Hunting, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, Toomai of the Elephants and Tiger! Tiger! Seeonee. India. Voice and tone: warm, adventurous and a little wild, like a story told by a fire. Dangers are real but never gory: deaths are stated plainly and gently; the tiger dies when the buffalo herd stampedes.
chapters: A Boy at the Village Door

beats.scene: Father Wolf stretches at the mouth of his cave as the sun sets
beats.summary: At dusk in the Seeonee hills, Father Wolf wakes and stretches in his cave.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf lies with four tumbling cubs in the dark cave
beats.summary: Mother Wolf lies beside her four cubs while the jungle wakes for the night.

beats.scene: A thin jackal peers into the cave mouth at dusk
beats.summary: Tabaqui the jackal arrives at the cave, and Father Wolf welcomes him coldly.

beats.scene: Tabaqui cracks a bone on the cave floor and grins
beats.summary: Tabaqui cracks a dry bone and cheerfully says that Shere Khan has moved his hunting ground to the Seeonee hills.

beats.scene: Father Wolf bristles at the cave mouth while Mother Wolf looks scornful
beats.summary: Father Wolf says that the tiger has no right to change his hunting ground without warning, and that his lame foot makes him a poor hunter.

beats.scene: Far below the cave a huge tiger roars angrily in the dark jungle
beats.summary: A loud, angry whine echoes through the valley: Shere Khan has missed his kill.

beats.scene: A small brown baby crawls out of the bushes toward the cave
beats.summary: A naked human baby crawls up to the cave, and Father Wolf stops in the middle of his spring.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf watches as the baby snuggles in among the wolf cubs
beats.summary: Mother Wolf calls for the child to be brought in, and he settles among her cubs without fear.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf licks the baby's face and holds him close
beats.summary: Mother Wolf decides to keep the baby and names him Mowgli the Frog, because he has no hair.

beats.scene: The giant head of a tiger fills the moonlit mouth of the cave
beats.summary: Shere Khan's huge head and shoulders fill the cave mouth, and his voice demands the man's cub.

beats.scene: Shere Khan glares into the cave while Mother Wolf shields the baby
beats.summary: Shere Khan demands the man's cub, and Mother Wolf refuses.

beats.scene: The tiger snarls at the narrow cave mouth, too big to squeeze inside
beats.summary: The cave is too small for a tiger, and Shere Khan leaves, swearing that the Pack will decide.

beats.scene: The wolf family walks up a moonlit hillside toward a flat rock
beats.summary: Father Wolf says the Pack must see the cub, and the family carries him to Council Rock.

beats.scene: Wolves gather around the great flat rock beneath a full moon
beats.summary: The wolves of the Pack gather at Council Rock, and Akela, the grey leader, lies on his stone.

beats.scene: A naked baby plays with pebbles in the moonlight among wolves
beats.summary: Mowgli sits in the circle and plays with pebbles while the wolves look on.

beats.scene: Akela calls to the Pack from his rock as Shere Khan appears
beats.summary: Akela calls the old words, "Look well, O Wolves", and Shere Khan steps forward to claim the cub.

beats.scene: Akela looks around the silent ring of wolves
beats.summary: Akela asks who speaks for the cub, since the Law says two members of the Pack who are not his parents must speak.

beats.scene: Baloo the brown bear stands up on his hind legs
beats.summary: Baloo, the old brown bear who teaches the Law to the young wolves, rises and speaks for the child.

beats.scene: Bagheera the black panther glides into the ring beside a fresh bull
beats.summary: Bagheera, the black panther, speaks for the cub and buys his place with a bull he killed that evening.

beats.scene: The Pack howls approval while Shere Khan stalks off, angry in the dark
beats.summary: The Pack accepts Mowgli, and Shere Khan stalks away, swearing to come back for him.

beats.scene: A brown child and four wolf cubs tumble together outside the cave
beats.summary: Mowgli grows up in the wolf family, playing and eating with his brothers.

beats.scene: Father Wolf crouches beside Mowgli in the dark jungle and points
beats.summary: Father Wolf teaches Mowgli what every rustle, call and splash in the jungle means.

beats.scene: Mowgli and Gray Brother climb a tree beside a river
beats.summary: Mowgli runs, climbs and swims with Gray Brother, the eldest of the cubs.

beats.scene: Baloo the brown bear lectures Mowgli beside a river
beats.summary: Baloo, the old bear, teaches Mowgli the Law of the Jungle and cuffs him when he forgets.

beats.scene: Mowgli repeats his lesson while Baloo nods under a shady tree
beats.summary: Baloo teaches Mowgli the Master-Words, which let him speak to every jungle people in peace.

beats.scene: Bagheera lies along a high branch with half-closed eyes
beats.summary: Bagheera the panther, who loves Mowgli, lies on a branch and listens while Mowgli recites.

beats.scene: Bagheera shows Mowgli a bare patch of fur under his throat
beats.summary: Bagheera tells Mowgli that he was born among men, in a king's cage at Oodeypore, and escaped.

beats.scene: Bagheera sits in the tree and tells Mowgli a story with solemn eyes
beats.summary: Bagheera says that Mowgli bought his place in the Pack with a bull, and that Shere Khan still hates him.

beats.scene: Baloo sits grumpily in the mud with leaves on his head
beats.summary: Baloo warns Mowgli never to speak with the Monkey People, who have no Law and no memory.

beats.scene: Mowgli sulks beneath a thorny bush while Baloo scowls
beats.summary: Mowgli gets tired of lessons and says he does not need all this teaching, and Baloo cuffs him.

beats.scene: Mowgli sits alone in a green glade weaving branches
beats.summary: Alone and sore, Mowgli sits in a glade and weaves a shelter out of branches and vines.

beats.scene: Grey monkeys peer down from the branches overhead
beats.summary: The Monkey People appear in the branches, chattering, and Mowgli remembers Baloo's warning.

beats.scene: Monkeys cheer and wave their arms while one hangs by its tail
beats.summary: The monkeys boast that they are great, free and wonderful, and they praise Mowgli's weaving.

beats.scene: Many hands reach for Mowgli's arms and legs in a tree
beats.summary: Without warning, the monkeys seize Mowgli by the arms and legs and swing off with him.

beats.scene: Monkeys leap from tree to tree carrying a boy high above the jungle
beats.summary: The monkeys race through the treetops with Mowgli, leaping from branch to branch at dizzying speed.

beats.scene: A hawk-like kite circles in the blue sky above the treetops
beats.summary: Mowgli sees Chil the kite circling above and remembers the Master-Word for the kites.

beats.scene: Mowgli shouts to the circling kite while monkeys carry him along
beats.summary: Mowgli calls the Master-Word to Chil and asks him to tell Baloo and Bagheera where he is going.

beats.scene: Chil the kite dives low over the hills toward the bear and the panther
beats.summary: Chil flies back to the hills, finds Baloo and Bagheera, and tells them that the Monkey People have taken the boy.

beats.scene: Baloo hangs his head while Bagheera glares at him in the dusk
beats.summary: Baloo is ashamed that he struck Mowgli, and Bagheera, angry and anxious, says that the Bandar-log are too many and too fast to fight alone.

beats.scene: Bagheera thinks on a rock while Baloo shakes his head
beats.summary: Bagheera says that only Kaa the python is feared by the monkeys, and Baloo agrees to ask for his help.

beats.scene: Baloo and Bagheera hurry through tall grass at the edge of a rocky valley
beats.summary: Bagheera tells Baloo what he knows about Kaa as they hurry over the rocks to find him.

beats.scene: A huge patterned snake lies gleaming on a warm rock in the sun
beats.summary: They find Kaa lying on a sunlit rock, admiring his bright new skin.

beats.scene: Bagheera bows politely before the enormous coiled python
beats.summary: Bagheera and Baloo greet Kaa politely, since a python who has just shed his skin is hungry and slow to anger.

beats.scene: Kaa's flat head turns toward the visitors while the sun lights his skin
beats.summary: Bagheera flatters Kaa on his new skin, and Kaa grows friendly and asks what they want.

beats.scene: Kaa listens while Baloo explains with a worried face
beats.summary: Baloo and Bagheera tell Kaa that the Bandar-log have taken the man-cub, and Kaa hisses with anger.

beats.scene: Kaa curls into a tight angry coil while rustling leaves fall
beats.summary: Kaa says the monkeys call him a yellow earth-worm and a snake without teeth, and that he will hunt them gladly.

beats.scene: Kaa asks questions while Bagheera shows him the way to the north
beats.summary: Kaa asks about the man-cub, and when he hears that the boy knew the Master-Word, he agrees that the boy is a friend.

beats.scene: A panther, a bear and a huge python cross a dark river in moonlight
beats.summary: As night falls, Kaa, Baloo and Bagheera set out and travel fast through the night, with Chil the kite guiding them.

beats.scene: Weathered stone walls rise out of the trees in moonlight
beats.summary: The three reach the hills above the Cold Lairs and see the old walls of a ruined city.

beats.scene: Kaa slides toward the wall while Baloo and Bagheera look back at him
beats.summary: Kaa tells the others to go first and fight, and he will come by a quieter road to reach the monkeys unseen.

beats.scene: Monkeys drag a boy through crumbling stone gates into a ruined city
beats.summary: Meanwhile the monkeys bring Mowgli to the Cold Lairs, a ruined city overgrown with trees.

beats.scene: Monkeys crowd around Mowgli in an overgrown courtyard, all chattering
beats.summary: The monkeys boast loudly about how clever and strong they are, and Mowgli grows tired and hungry.

beats.scene: A monkey drops a nut, forgets it and leaps away
beats.summary: Mowgli sees that the monkeys cannot keep their minds on anything: they begin a plan, forget it and start another.

beats.scene: Mowgli walks along a crumbling wall at dusk, searching for a gap
beats.summary: Mowgli looks for a way out of the city, but the walls are high and the monkeys hold him back.

beats.scene: Stars come out over an old stone city while a boy waits
beats.summary: As night comes, Mowgli sits on a terrace and trusts that Chil's message has reached Baloo and Bagheera.

beats.scene: A black panther leaps over the wall into a swarm of monkeys
beats.summary: Bagheera bursts into the city and attacks the monkeys, who swarm over him by the hundred.

beats.scene: A black panther rolls into a pool beneath a mound of grey monkeys
beats.summary: The monkeys pile onto Bagheera until he rolls into the water tank, where they cannot follow him closely.

beats.scene: A big brown bear swings his paws among leaping monkeys
beats.summary: Baloo arrives and fights with his great paws, but the monkeys overwhelm him too.

beats.scene: Monkeys push a boy through a doorway into a small dark summer-house
beats.summary: The monkeys seize Mowgli and push him into the old summer-house, a roofless marble pavilion, to keep him from the fight.

beats.scene: A boy peers through a crack in stone toward a courtyard full of monkeys
beats.summary: Through the cracks, Mowgli sees his friends buried under monkeys, and hears a faint hiss beyond the wall.

beats.scene: A huge shadow slides silently along the top of a moonlit wall
beats.summary: Kaa slides along the top of the wall, and the monkeys nearest to him fall silent.

beats.scene: A huge snake's head strikes a marble wall, which cracks open
beats.summary: Kaa strikes the wall of the summer-house with his great head until the marble breaks and Mowgli can see out.

beats.scene: Mowgli stands in the broken wall beside the head of a giant snake
beats.summary: Mowgli greets Kaa with the Master-Word, and Kaa tells him to stay back and watch.

beats.scene: Kaa rises in the moonlight and begins to sway before hundreds of monkeys
beats.summary: Kaa begins the Dance of Hunger, swaying slowly from side to side in the moonlight.

beats.scene: A crowd of monkeys stares upward without moving, mouths open
beats.summary: The monkeys cannot look away from the dancing snake, and they stand still, frozen and staring.

beats.scene: A panther climbs out of a pool, staring at a swaying snake
beats.summary: Mowgli sees that Bagheera, climbing out of the tank, and Baloo are also caught by the dance and are walking toward Kaa.

beats.scene: A boy shakes a panther and a bear by their shoulders
beats.summary: Mowgli runs among the dazed monkeys and pulls Baloo and Bagheera back, shaking them until they wake.

beats.scene: Baloo and Bagheera sit ashamed beside a boy in the shadow of a wall
beats.summary: Bagheera and Baloo are ashamed, and they thank Mowgli for saving them from the dance.

beats.scene: Monkeys vanish into the dark as Kaa curls among the ruins
beats.summary: Kaa has his meal, and the monkeys who were caught by the dance are never seen again; the rest flee in terror.

beats.scene: Four friends walk away through the gate of a ruined city at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Mowgli thanks Kaa, and the friends set out for home.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf hugs Mowgli at the mouth of the cave while wolf cubs watch
beats.summary: Mowgli comes home to the cave, and Mother Wolf scolds him and holds him close.

beats.scene: Mowgli, grown taller, stares at a wolf who looks down
beats.summary: Years pass, and Mowgli grows strong and tall, and learns to stare down any wolf of the Pack.

beats.scene: Gray Brother whispers to Mowgli among tall dry grass at dusk
beats.summary: Gray Brother warns Mowgli that Shere Khan is whispering to the young wolves against him.

beats.scene: Bagheera lies in a shady hollow beside Mowgli and speaks quietly
beats.summary: Bagheera confirms the danger: Akela is growing old, and when he misses his kill, the young wolves will turn on him and on Mowgli.

beats.scene: Bagheera points toward the far-off lights of a village in the dusk
beats.summary: Bagheera tells Mowgli to fetch the Red Flower, the thing that all the jungle fears, from the village of men.

beats.scene: Mowgli looks at Bagheera with calm eyes under a big banyan tree
beats.summary: Mowgli is not afraid of men and agrees to fetch the Red Flower, because he has heard it can be fed with sticks.

beats.scene: A small boy crouches behind a bush watching a village at night
beats.summary: At night Mowgli runs through the forest to the edge of the village and watches the huts from the shadows.

beats.scene: A boy lifts a glowing clay pot from the doorway of a hut
beats.summary: Mowgli finds a clay pot full of glowing coals at the door of a hut and carries it away.

beats.scene: A boy runs through dark trees with a glowing pot and dry sticks
beats.summary: Mowgli runs back through the jungle, feeding the fire with sticks and bark so that it does not die.

beats.scene: A black panther sits waiting on a rock as a boy arrives with fire
beats.summary: Bagheera, waiting on a rock, is amazed at Mowgli's pot of fire, and tells him that it will be his weapon against Shere Khan.

beats.scene: A pack of wolves chases a deer across a moonlit meadow
beats.summary: The Pack hunts a buck at night, and old Akela makes the leap but misses.

beats.scene: Old Akela lies alone on a high rock, head on his paws
beats.summary: Akela knows what his miss means, and lies alone on his rock, while Shere Khan whispers to the young wolves.

beats.scene: Wolves gather in a ring around the Council Rock at night
beats.summary: The Pack gathers at Council Rock, with Shere Khan lying at the side.

beats.scene: Old grey Akela stands before the ring of wolves, speaking calmly
beats.summary: Akela says that he has led the Pack for years and has the right to be killed fairly, but let any wolf come and fight him.

beats.scene: Shere Khan looms over the ring and points at the old wolf
beats.summary: Shere Khan says that Akela is finished, and demands that the man-cub, whom the Pack bought with a bull, be given to him.

beats.scene: A boy walks out of the dark carrying a burning branch
beats.summary: Mowgli walks into the circle, carrying a burning branch from his Red Flower, and the wolves shrink back.

beats.scene: A boy swings a flaming branch at the head of a tiger
beats.summary: Mowgli swings the burning branch and beats Shere Khan, who howls and runs from the circle.

beats.scene: Mowgli stands in front of old Akela with the fire in his hand
beats.summary: Mowgli shields Akela and warns the Pack that he will burn any wolf who touches him.

beats.scene: A boy weeps at the edge of the Council Rock, wolves watching
beats.summary: Mowgli, who has decided to leave the Pack, weeps for the first time and learns that these drops are tears.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf and Father Wolf stand at the cave while a boy hugs them
beats.summary: Mowgli says goodbye to his wolf family, and promises that he will bring back Shere Khan's skin.

beats.scene: Muddy flood water carries a small animal through a ditch in the rain
beats.summary: In a rainy summer in India, a flood washes a young mongoose out of his burrow and carries him down a ditch.

beats.scene: A small boy kneels over a wet, limp animal on a garden path
beats.summary: Teddy, a small boy, finds the half-drowned mongoose on the path and thinks that he is dead.

beats.scene: A man kneels on the veranda holding a mongoose wrapped in cotton wool
beats.summary: Teddy's father sees that the mongoose is still breathing, and the family dries him and warms him in cotton wool.

beats.scene: A mongoose sits on a boy's shoulder as the family eats breakfast
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki recovers quickly and shows that he is not afraid of people, for the motto of his family is "run and find out".

beats.scene: A small animal peers into an ink bottle on a writing table
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki explores the bungalow, running over the desk, the lamps and the bathroom, and gets inkwell on his nose.

beats.scene: A woman looks anxiously at a mongoose as her husband smiles
beats.summary: Teddy's mother worries about a wild animal in the nursery, but her husband says a mongoose will keep the snakes away.

beats.scene: A small mongoose stands among rose bushes in a sunny, wild garden
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki walks into the big garden, full of roses, lemon trees and tall bamboos, and meets a fine place for hunting.

beats.scene: A small bird weeps beside a tiny nest of sewn leaves in a bush
beats.summary: In the garden Rikki-Tikki meets Darzee the tailorbird, crying because a snake has taken one of his babies.

beats.scene: Darzee points at the long grass while his wife hides in the leaves
beats.summary: Darzee tells Rikki-Tikki that Nag and Nagaina, two great cobras, live in the garden and hunt there.

beats.scene: A huge cobra rises from the grass with its hood spread wide
beats.summary: Nag rises from the grass, and Rikki-Tikki stands his ground, even while Nagaina creeps up behind him.

beats.scene: A small animal leaps into the air as a cobra strikes the empty ground
beats.summary: At Darzee's cry Rikki-Tikki jumps high, Nagaina's strike misses him, and the two cobras slide away into the grass.

beats.scene: A boy plays on a path while a small snake creeps near
beats.summary: Next day Teddy plays on the path, and Rikki-Tikki sees a tiny dusty brown snake, a Karait, creeping toward the boy's hand.

beats.scene: A mongoose fights a small snake in a cloud of dust beside a boy
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki leaps at the Karait and kills it, and Teddy's parents are delighted that the mongoose has saved him.

beats.scene: A shy muskrat creeps along the wall of a dark bedroom at night
beats.summary: That night Rikki-Tikki meets Chuchundra the muskrat, who never dares to cross the middle of the floor.

beats.scene: A trembling muskrat whispers to a mongoose in the dark
beats.summary: Chuchundra is too frightened to say what he has heard, but he whispers that Nag is in the garden and means to come in.

beats.scene: A mongoose hides behind a big water jar in a dark bathroom
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki goes to the bathroom, hides behind the big water jar, and waits for Nag to appear at the drain.

beats.scene: A huge cobra slides through a wall hole and coils by the jar
beats.summary: After a long wait, Nag slides through the hole and coils round the water jar, whispering to Nagaina that they will rule the garden once the people are gone.

beats.scene: A mongoose clings to the head of a thrashing cobra
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki jumps on Nag's head and holds on, even when the cobra whips him around the bathroom.

beats.scene: A man in a nightshirt aims a gun at a struggling snake
beats.summary: Teddy's father rushes in with a gun and shoots Nag, and the great cobra falls dead.

beats.scene: A woman lifts a tired mongoose into a bed beside a sleeping boy
beats.summary: Teddy's mother takes Rikki-Tikki to bed, and in the morning Darzee sings that Nag is dead, but Rikki-Tikki remembers Nagaina.

beats.scene: A mongoose scolds a singing tailorbird on a branch
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki scolds Darzee for singing too early, because Nagaina is still alive and her eggs are hidden somewhere.

beats.scene: A mongoose and a tailorbird whisper at the edge of a melon bed
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki asks where Nagaina keeps her eggs, and Darzee says they are in the melon bed at the end nearest the wall.

beats.scene: A mother bird flutters along the ground, dragging one wing
beats.summary: Darzee's clever wife pretends to have a broken wing and leads Nagaina away from the melon bed.

beats.scene: A mongoose digs among the leaves of a melon bed in the sun
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki finds the nest of eggs in the melon bed and destroys all of them except one.

beats.scene: A bird cries out in terror beside a veranda full of morning light
beats.summary: Darzee's wife cries out that Nagaina has left her and gone to the bungalow to kill the people.

beats.scene: A cobra raises her hood above a small boy on a veranda
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki reaches the veranda and finds Nagaina coiled on the matting next to Teddy, ready to strike.

beats.scene: A mongoose holds a white egg before a hissing cobra
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki calls to Nagaina and shows her the last egg, and she turns toward it and begs him to give it back.

beats.scene: A cobra grabs a pale egg and slithers off the veranda
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki rolls the egg toward the edge of the veranda, Nagaina snatches it, and Teddy's father pulls his son to safety.

beats.scene: A mongoose plunges into the dark entrance of a hole in the ground
beats.summary: Nagaina races to her hole under the bush, and Rikki-Tikki dives in after her, into the dark.

beats.scene: A tired mongoose climbs out of a hole while a bird sings above
beats.summary: After a long silence, Rikki-Tikki comes out and says that it is all over, and from that day the cobras never trouble the garden again.

beats.scene: A camp of grass huts and tame elephants on a forested hillside
beats.summary: In the hills of India there is a camp where working elephants live with their drivers, and one boy is growing up there.

beats.scene: A ten-year-old boy stands proudly with his father in a camp
beats.summary: Little Toomai, a ten-year-old boy, is the son and grandson of elephant drivers, and he wants to follow them.

beats.scene: A huge old elephant stands under a tree, his tusks gleaming
beats.summary: Kala Nag, Black Snake, is the old working elephant that Big Toomai drives, as strong and wise as any in the camp.

beats.scene: A small boy washes a giant elephant in a shining river
beats.summary: Little Toomai loves Kala Nag, and every morning he helps wash him in the river and feeds him sugar-cane.

beats.scene: Elephants stand in a line with ropes around their legs
beats.summary: In the camp's lines stand the other elephants, among them Pudmini, and every one of them knows Little Toomai.

beats.scene: Wild elephants are driven by men into a huge wooden fence
beats.summary: The Government catches wild elephants by driving whole herds into a great fenced yard, the Keddah, and Kala Nag helps.

beats.scene: A boy pleads with his father beside a huge elephant
beats.summary: Little Toomai begs his father to be allowed to go with the men to the Keddah, but Big Toomai says he is too young.

beats.scene: A tall white man in a hat inspects a long line of elephants
beats.summary: Petersen Sahib, the white officer who runs the elephant catching, visits the lines and notices the boy.

beats.scene: A tall man laughs kindly at a boy standing by an elephant
beats.summary: Petersen Sahib hears that the boy wants to catch elephants, and jokes that he will be a hunter when he has seen the elephants dance.

beats.scene: A boy sits alone on the ground looking up at old hunters
beats.summary: Little Toomai asks the drivers where the elephants dance, and the old men laugh and say that no one has ever seen it.

beats.scene: Drivers sit around a campfire at night with the elephants behind them
beats.summary: One evening the drivers eat their rice around the campfire while the tame elephants doze nearby.

beats.scene: An old man with a white beard speaks to the fire-lit faces
beats.summary: An old driver tells of the secret dance, where wild elephants gather in the jungle on nights of the full moon.

beats.scene: Elephants walk single file through trees toward a distant hill
beats.summary: The old man says that the dancing ground is a bare, hard place on a hilltop, trodden flat by the feet of many elephants.

beats.scene: Big Toomai laughs and shakes his head beside the fire
beats.summary: Big Toomai laughs and says that no man has ever seen the dance and lived to tell it, but Little Toomai believes.

beats.scene: A small boy lies on straw beside a huge sleeping elephant
beats.summary: Little Toomai goes to bed beside Kala Nag, listening to the sounds of the camp and looking at the stars.

beats.scene: A great elephant lifts his head and spreads his ears in the dark
beats.summary: Kala Nag does not lie down to sleep; he stands with his head raised and his ears spread wide, listening.

beats.scene: A boy sits up in the dark, listening to a far-off sound
beats.summary: From the hills comes a faint sound like a heavy drum, and Little Toomai sits up to listen.

beats.scene: A huge elephant tugs at a heavy iron chain fixed to a wooden peg
beats.summary: Kala Nag pulls at the chain that holds him to the peg, again and again, until the peg comes out of the ground.

beats.scene: A boy climbs up the trunk of an elephant onto his neck
beats.summary: Little Toomai grabs the elephant's ear and scrambles up onto his neck, determined not to be left behind.

beats.scene: A great elephant walks silently away from a sleeping camp into dark trees
beats.summary: Kala Nag walks out of the sleeping camp and into the jungle, with Little Toomai on his neck, making no more noise than a breeze in the grass.

beats.scene: A boy lies low on an elephant's neck as branches pass overhead
beats.summary: Kala Nag climbs steadily through the dark forest, and Little Toomai lies low on his neck to avoid the branches.

beats.scene: A second huge elephant steps out of the shadows beside the first
beats.summary: A second elephant comes out of the shadows and falls in beside Kala Nag, and then a third.

beats.scene: A herd of elephants walks through a moonlit forest in single file
beats.summary: More and more elephants join them from every side, until the boy rides in the middle of a moving river of grey backs.

beats.scene: Elephants climb a bare moonlit hill toward a round clearing
beats.summary: The herd climbs a long slope and comes out on a bare hilltop, a round clearing where the ground is trodden as hard as stone.

beats.scene: Many elephants stand in a ring on bare ground under the moon
beats.summary: The elephants gather in the clearing, and Kala Nag takes his place among them while Little Toomai holds his breath.

beats.scene: Elephants rock from side to side and stamp their feet in the moonlight
beats.summary: The dance begins, as the elephants rock from side to side and stamp their huge feet in time.

beats.scene: Tusks flash and dust rises as elephants stamp in circles
beats.summary: The elephants circle and stamp for hours, the dust rising in clouds, and Little Toomai feels the drumming in his bones.

beats.scene: A boy clings to an elephant's neck as the moon sinks lower
beats.summary: The hours pass, the moon sinks, and the dance slows until at last it comes to an end.

beats.scene: A tired boy sleeps on the neck of an elephant walking home
beats.summary: At dawn the herd melts back into the jungle, and Kala Nag carries the sleeping boy home to the camp.

beats.scene: Men cheer around a boy and an elephant as an officer smiles
beats.summary: The drivers follow the trail to the dancing ground, and Petersen Sahib names the boy Toomai of the Elephants.

beats.scene: A tall boy walks across green hills toward a thin column of smoke
beats.summary: Mowgli walks over the hills at dawn toward the village of men, with the smoke of its fires in the distance.

beats.scene: Villagers stare at a barefoot boy at the edge of a village
beats.summary: Mowgli reaches the village, and the people stare at the barefoot boy with long black hair who does not speak their language.

beats.scene: A kind woman with a worn face kneels in a doorway
beats.summary: A woman called Messua comes out of her hut, looks into his face, and cries out that he is like the son she lost.

beats.scene: A woman holds out a bowl of milk to a boy in a doorway
beats.summary: Messua welcomes the boy into her house, gives him milk and food, and asks no questions.

beats.scene: A boy lies awake in a small, dark mud hut at night
beats.summary: That night Mowgli sleeps in a house for the first time, and the roof and walls feel like a trap, so he moves to the doorway.

beats.scene: A woman points at objects while a boy repeats the words
beats.summary: Day after day Messua teaches Mowgli the words of men, and he learns quickly because he has learned the speech of every jungle people.

beats.scene: Village boys laugh and race a barefoot boy along a dusty lane
beats.summary: The village boys laugh at Mowgli's strange ways, but he outruns every one of them, and soon they stop laughing.

beats.scene: A boastful hunter with an old gun speaks to villagers by the fire
beats.summary: Buldeo, the village hunter, tells wild tales of the jungle by the fire, and Mowgli laughs when he hears one about a wolf-boy.

beats.scene: A boy sits on the back of a huge black water buffalo
beats.summary: The headman sends Mowgli out to herd the village buffaloes with the other boys, and he finds that he likes the work.

beats.scene: A great black bull stands in a muddy pool while a boy watches
beats.summary: At the head of the herd is Rama, a great bull, who takes the boy's measure and decides to obey him.

beats.scene: Buffaloes lie in a river at noon while boys sit on their backs
beats.summary: In the heat of the day the herd lies in the river up to the nostrils, and Mowgli and the herd boys doze on their backs.

beats.scene: A boy talks softly to a calf while the herd grazes in a meadow
beats.summary: Mowgli grows fond of the herd, and he finds that he can talk to the buffaloes in a language of his own.

beats.scene: A grey wolf stands in long grass at the edge of a field
beats.summary: One evening Gray Brother comes out of the grass at the edge of the field to find Mowgli.

beats.scene: A wolf whispers in the grass beside a boy at twilight
beats.summary: Gray Brother warns Mowgli that Shere Khan has been hiding in the ravine near the village for many days, waiting for him.

beats.scene: Steep rocky walls close in on a narrow valley with one open end
beats.summary: Mowgli is not afraid, and he sees that the ravine, a narrow valley with steep walls, could be a trap for the tiger.

beats.scene: A boy and a wolf crouch behind a boulder and talk quietly
beats.summary: Mowgli tells Gray Brother his plan: the whole buffalo herd will be driven down the ravine, and Gray Brother must fetch Akela.

beats.scene: A grey wolf runs away through tall grass under a darkening sky
beats.summary: Gray Brother runs through the night to fetch Akela, and Mowgli promises to meet them at dawn at the top of the ravine.

beats.scene: A boy lies awake on a village roof looking at the night sky
beats.summary: That night Mowgli lies awake, thinking of the tiger and the Pack, and his heart is quiet.

beats.scene: Villagers watch a boy lead a herd of black buffaloes out at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Mowgli takes the whole herd out of the village, though the other boys offer to come, and he tells them to stay behind.

beats.scene: Two wolves wait among the rocks at the top of a ravine
beats.summary: At the head of the ravine Gray Brother and old Akela are waiting, and Akela greets Mowgli with a low bow.

beats.scene: A boy on a great black bull looks down into a deep, narrow valley
beats.summary: From the top of the ravine Mowgli looks down and sees the striped shape of Shere Khan lying in the shadows below.

beats.scene: Two wolves drive half of a buffalo herd away along the hillside
beats.summary: Akela and Gray Brother cut the herd in two, and the wolves drive one half around the hill to the lower end of the valley.

beats.scene: A boy waits quietly on a black bull while the sun climbs
beats.summary: Mowgli waits on the bull while the wolves get into position, and the sun climbs slowly over the hills.

beats.scene: A boy calls down into a ravine with a hand cupped to his mouth
beats.summary: Mowgli calls down to Shere Khan, using the tiger's own name for himself, and tells him that the man-cub he hunted is here.

beats.scene: A great tiger rises in a narrow valley, staring up in surprise
beats.summary: Shere Khan wakes, rises to his feet and looks up, and then he looks down the valley and understands that he is caught.

beats.scene: A tiger leaps at a steep rock wall and slides back down
beats.summary: Shere Khan tries to climb the steep walls of the ravine, but he is lame and the rock is smooth, and he slides back.

beats.scene: A boy raises his arm on a great bull at the edge
beats.summary: Mowgli raises his arm and shouts the old call to the herd, and Rama leaps forward with the bulls behind him.

beats.scene: A river of horns and dust pours down a narrow rocky valley
beats.summary: The herd thunders down the ravine like a flood of horns and dust, while the other half comes up from the bottom.

beats.scene: A cloud of dust drifts over a silent ravine floor
beats.summary: Shere Khan is trapped between the two halves of the herd, and the great hunter's long hunt for the man-cub ends there.

beats.scene: A boy stands in the quiet ravine beside a great striped tiger
beats.summary: Mowgli rides down, finds that the herd has calmed, and stands beside the great tiger, remembering his promise at Council Rock.

beats.scene: A boy kneels with a knife beside a tiger while two wolves watch
beats.summary: Mowgli takes out his knife and carefully skins the tiger, as he had seen the village men do, while the wolves watch.

beats.scene: A heavy old man with a long gun puffs up a rocky track
beats.summary: While Mowgli works, Buldeo the old hunter comes puffing up the track with his long gun, looking for a stray buffalo.

beats.scene: A hunter holds out a hand for a tiger skin
beats.summary: Buldeo sees that the tiger is dead and demands that the skin be given to him, so that he can claim the reward.

beats.scene: A calm boy shakes his head, holding a tiger skin
beats.summary: Mowgli politely refuses: the skin is promised to the Council Rock, and he did not kill the tiger for a reward.

beats.scene: Two grey wolves rise up from the rocks behind a frightened man
beats.summary: Buldeo raises his gun, but two grey wolves rise from the rocks behind him, and he drops it in fear.

beats.scene: A terrified man runs away down a hillside, waving his arms
beats.summary: Buldeo runs back to the village, shouting that Mowgli is a sorcerer who speaks with wolves and has called them to kill him.

beats.scene: A boy drives a herd of buffaloes toward a distant village at dusk
beats.summary: Mowgli rolls up the skin, shoulders it, and drives the herd back toward the village, not yet knowing what Buldeo has said.

beats.scene: Angry men with sticks and stones gather at the village gate
beats.summary: When Mowgli reaches the village, a crowd of angry men with sticks are waiting at the gate, and they call him a sorcerer.

beats.scene: Villagers throw stones at a boy carrying a tiger skin
beats.summary: The villagers shut their doors against him and throw stones, and Mowgli walks on through the street without lifting a hand.

beats.scene: A kind woman weeps in a doorway as a boy passes in the dusk
beats.summary: Messua weeps at her door, but she is powerless to help him, and the boy she had hoped to call her son vanishes into the dusk.

beats.scene: A boy with a tiger skin on his shoulder walks into a dark forest
beats.summary: Mowgli walks out of the village through the night, and when he reaches the dark edge of the jungle, he feels the old smells welcome him.

beats.scene: A grey wolf runs beside a boy through moonlit trees
beats.summary: Akela and Gray Brother catch up with him in the forest, and the three of them go home together toward the Seeonee hills.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf licks a boy's face at the mouth of a cave at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Mowgli reaches the cave where he was raised, and Mother Wolf and Father Wolf welcome him home.

beats.scene: Mowgli sits at the cave mouth telling a story as wolves listen
beats.summary: Mowgli tells the family how he has killed Shere Khan, and Mother Wolf says that she always knew that he would keep his promise.

beats.scene: A boy spreads a striped skin on a flat rock in the red sunset
beats.summary: At sunset Mowgli goes to Council Rock and spreads the tiger's skin upon it, weighing down its edges with stones.

beats.scene: A boy stands on a great rock and calls to the hills
beats.summary: Mowgli calls the Pack together with the old cry, and the wolves come running from every part of the hills.

beats.scene: Wolves stare at a striped tiger skin spread on a flat rock
beats.summary: The wolves look at the skin, and there is a long silence, and then a great cry of welcome rises.

beats.scene: A boy stands before wolves, shaking his head with a smile
beats.summary: The wolves ask Mowgli to be their leader, but he refuses, saying that he would rather run with them as a brother.

beats.scene: Wolves sit in a circle around a boy singing on a tiger skin
beats.summary: Mowgli stands on the skin and sings of the hunt, Baloo and Bagheera arrive to join the feast, and the whole Pack howls its joy.

beats.scene: A boy runs through a moonlit forest with his wolf brothers
beats.summary: Mowgli runs through the moonlit jungle with his wolf brothers, at home at last, among the friends who raised him.

A1A2: At sunset, Father Wolf woke up in his cave on the hill.
Mother Wolf lay beside him with her four small cubs.
A thin wild dog named Tabaqui came to the cave door.
Tabaqui ate an old bone and said, “Shere Khan is coming.”
Father Wolf was angry because the tiger had come without asking.
A loud, angry cry came up from the dark valley.
Something moved in the bushes, and a small brown baby crawled out.
The baby went in the cave and lay down with the cubs.
Mother Wolf said, “I will keep him and call him Mowgli.”
Suddenly a huge tiger's head filled the mouth of the cave.
Shere Khan said that the man's cub was his and he wanted it.
The cave was too small for him, so the tiger went away.
Father Wolf said the Pack must see the child, and he carried him.
The Pack gathered around the rock, and Akela lay on top.
The baby sat in the moonlight and played with small stones.
Akela called, “Look well, O wolves, and tell me what you see.”
Akela said, “Who will speak for the man's cub?”
Baloo, the old brown bear, stood up and spoke.
Bagheera the panther offered a fat young bull for the boy.
The wolves said yes, and Shere Khan went away angry.
Mowgli grew up in the cave with his four wolf brothers.
Father Wolf taught him what every sound in the jungle meant.
Mowgli ran and swam with Gray Brother every day.
Baloo taught Mowgli the Law of the Jungle each day.
Baloo taught him words that every jungle animal would know.
Bagheera the panther watched him from a high branch.
Bagheera said, “I was born among men, in a cage.”
Bagheera said, “The Pack knows you, but the tiger wants you.”
Baloo said, “Never talk to the Monkey People.”
Mowgli was tired of lessons, and Baloo gave him a cuff.
Mowgli sat alone in the forest and made a small house.
Many monkeys came to the trees and watched him work.
The monkeys shouted that they were great and free and wonderful.
Suddenly, many hands took hold of Mowgli and lifted him.
The monkeys jumped from tree to tree, carrying Mowgli high above the ground.
High above, Mowgli saw a big bird with wide wings.
Mowgli shouted the Master-Word, and the kite flew closer.
Chil flew fast over the hills to find Baloo and Bagheera.
Baloo was sad, and Bagheera was angry with him.
Bagheera said, “We must ask Kaa the python for help.”
Baloo and Bagheera ran fast over the rocks to find Kaa.
They found Kaa on a rock, with his new yellow skin.
Bagheera said politely, “Good hunting, Kaa.”
Kaa smiled when Bagheera said that his skin was beautiful.
Baloo told Kaa that the monkeys had taken Mowgli.
Kaa was angry because the monkeys called him a worm, and he wanted revenge.
Kaa asked about the man-cub, and then he nodded.
The three friends ran for hours, and Kaa kept up.
At last they saw big old walls above the trees.
Kaa told the others to go on first, and he would come quietly.
Meanwhile, the monkeys brought Mowgli to the old stone city.
Mowgli was hungry, but the monkeys only talked about themselves.
The monkeys forgot their plan and began a new game.
Mowgli looked for a way out, but the walls were high.
The night came, and Mowgli waited for his friends.
Bagheera leaped over the wall and into the city.
Bagheera fought hard, but the monkeys were too many.
Baloo came next, and he fought with his big paws.
The monkeys pushed Mowgli into an old stone house.
Mowgli looked through a crack and could not see his friends.
A huge shadow moved along the top of the wall.
Kaa hit the wall hard, and the old stone broke.
Mowgli said, “We be of one blood, ye and I.”
Kaa began to sway slowly in the moonlight.
The monkeys looked at Kaa and could not look away.
Mowgli saw that Bagheera and Baloo were walking toward Kaa.
Mowgli took hold of Baloo and Bagheera and pulled hard.
Bagheera said that Mowgli had saved them, and they were both very ashamed.
Kaa ate his meal, and the monkeys ran away in fear.
At dawn, Mowgli thanked Kaa, and the friends went home.
Mother Wolf held Mowgli close when he came home.
The years passed, and Mowgli grew tall and strong.
Gray Brother said, “Shere Khan is talking to the young wolves.”
Bagheera said, “Akela is old, and the Pack will turn on him.”
Bagheera said, “You must get the Red Flower.”
Mowgli said that he was not afraid of men, and he would go.
At night Mowgli went quietly near a village and watched the huts.
Mowgli found a clay pot of red fire and took it.
Mowgli fed the fire with sticks, and it grew bright.
Bagheera was amazed when he saw the pot of fire.
Akela jumped at the deer, but he missed.
Akela lay alone on his rock and felt very sad.
The Pack gathered at the rock, and Shere Khan was there.
Akela said that he had led them well, and they could try to kill him.
Shere Khan said that Akela was finished, and he asked for the man-cub.
Then Mowgli walked into the ring with a burning branch.
Mowgli hit Shere Khan with the fire, and the tiger ran.
Mowgli stood by Akela and said, “Do not touch him.”
Mowgli cried, and he did not know why.
Mowgli said goodbye and promised to bring back the tiger's skin.
A big flood carried a small animal called Rikki-Tikki away.
A small boy found Rikki-Tikki lying still on the path.
Teddy's father said that the little animal was not dead, only cold.
Rikki-Tikki sat on Teddy's shoulder and ate some fruit.
Rikki-Tikki ran all around the house to see everything.
Teddy's mother was afraid, but his father only smiled.
The garden was big, with roses, lemon trees and tall bamboo.
In the garden, Rikki-Tikki found a bird that was crying.
Darzee said, “Nag and Nagaina live in this garden.”
Suddenly, a huge black cobra rose out of the grass.
Rikki-Tikki jumped high, and the snake missed him.
A small brown snake was moving slowly toward Teddy on the path.
Rikki-Tikki jumped and killed the snake before it bit Teddy.
That night a shy little animal ran along the wall.
Chuchundra whispered, “Do not tell Nag that I spoke.”
Rikki-Tikki hid behind a big water jar and waited.
Finally, Nag came through the hole into the bathroom.
Rikki-Tikki jumped and took hold of Nag's head.
Teddy's father ran in with a gun and shot Nag.
In the morning, Darzee sang that Nag was dead.
Rikki-Tikki told Darzee to stop singing, because Nagaina was still alive.
Darzee said that the eggs were in the melon bed.
Darzee's wife acted as if her wing was broken.
Rikki-Tikki found the eggs and broke all but one.
Darzee's wife cried, “Nagaina has gone to the house!”
Nagaina sat next to Teddy, ready to strike.
Rikki-Tikki showed Nagaina her last egg and said that he had it.
Nagaina took the egg and slid away fast.
Nagaina went into her hole, and Rikki-Tikki followed.
At last Rikki-Tikki came out and said, “It is all over.”
In the hills there was a camp for the working elephants.
Little Toomai was ten, and his family drove elephants.
Kala Nag was the biggest and oldest elephant in the camp.
Every morning, Little Toomai washed Kala Nag in the river.
In the camp stood a line of big elephants, tied with ropes.
The men drove wild elephants into a big wooden yard.
Little Toomai asked his father, “May I go to the Keddah?”
Petersen Sahib, the officer, came to look at the elephants.
The officer said, “You will catch elephants when you see them dance.”
Little Toomai asked where elephants dance, but the men only laughed at him.
That evening, the drivers sat around the fire and ate rice.
An old driver said that wild elephants have a secret dance.
The old man said the elephants danced on a hard hill.
Big Toomai laughed, but Little Toomai believed every word the old man said.
Little Toomai lay down next to Kala Nag and looked at the stars.
Kala Nag did not sleep, but stood listening with his big ears wide.
Far away in the hills, a faint sound was heard.
Kala Nag pulled hard at his chain until the peg came out.
Little Toomai caught his ear and climbed up on his neck.
Kala Nag walked quietly out of the camp into the dark jungle.
Little Toomai held on tight while Kala Nag climbed through the forest.
Soon another elephant came out of the trees and walked beside them.
More and more elephants came out of the trees to join them.
At last they came to the top of a bare hill.
The elephants stood in the clearing, and the boy held his breath.
Then the elephants began to dance, and the ground shook.
The elephants stamped round and round, and the dust rose in clouds.
The hours passed, and the moon began to sink.
At dawn, Kala Nag walked home with the sleeping boy.
Petersen Sahib named the boy Toomai of the Elephants.
Mowgli walked across the hills toward the village at dawn.
The people of the village stared at the strange boy.
A kind woman came out and looked at his face.
Messua gave him milk and bread in her house.
That night Mowgli slept in a house for the first time.
Each day, Messua taught Mowgli new words, and he learned fast.
The village boys laughed at Mowgli, but he ran faster than all of them.
Old Buldeo told big stories about the jungle by the fire.
The village chief told Mowgli to look after the buffaloes.
The biggest buffalo was a bull called Rama.
At noon the buffaloes lay in the river, and the boys rested.
Mowgli grew fond of the buffaloes, and they understood him.
One evening, Gray Brother came out of the long grass.
Gray Brother said, “Shere Khan is waiting for you.”
The valley had steep walls, and it was a trap.
Mowgli told Gray Brother his plan, and Gray Brother listened.
Gray Brother ran off into the night to find Akela.
That night, Mowgli lay awake and thought about the tiger.
At dawn, Mowgli led the whole herd out of the village.
At the top of the valley, Akela and Gray Brother were waiting.
From the top, Mowgli looked down and saw Shere Khan.
The wolves cut the herd in two and drove half away.
Mowgli waited quietly while the sun rose higher.
Mowgli called out loudly, “Shere Khan, I am here!”
Shere Khan stood up and looked around in the shadows.
Shere Khan tried to climb the wall, but he slid back.
Mowgli raised his arm and gave a loud, wild cry.
The herd ran down the valley like a loud, black flood.
Shere Khan was trapped, and his long hunt was over.
Mowgli stood still beside the tiger and remembered his promise.
Mowgli took out his knife and began to skin the tiger.
Suddenly old Buldeo came along the path with his long gun.
Buldeo said that the skin was his, and he wanted it now.
Mowgli shook his head and said that the skin was not for sale.
Two big wolves stood up behind Buldeo, and he was afraid.
Buldeo ran back to the village, shouting about a wicked boy.
Mowgli rolled up the skin and took the herd home.
Angry men with sticks stood at the village gate.
The villagers threw stones at Mowgli as he walked on.
Messua wept at her door, but she could not help him.
Mowgli walked through the night, and the jungle welcomed him.
Akela and Gray Brother came to him, and they went home together.
At dawn, Mother Wolf and Father Wolf welcomed Mowgli home.
Mowgli told his wolf family how Shere Khan died.
At sunset, Mowgli put the tiger skin on the Council Rock.
Mowgli gave the old call, and the wolves came running.
The wolves looked at the skin, and then they cheered.
The wolves asked Mowgli to lead them, but he said no.
Mowgli sang on the tiger skin, and the wolves cried out with joy.
Mowgli ran with his wolf brothers, and the jungle was his home again.
B1B2: It was a warm evening in the Seeonee hills, and Father Wolf had just woken from his long day's sleep. He scratched his ear, yawned and spread his paws one by one to shake the sleep away.
Beside him lay Mother Wolf, grey and watchful, with her four cubs squeaking and tumbling against her side. Outside, the jungle was waking up, and the dusk was full of rustling and distant calls.
Just then a thin shadow fell across the cave mouth, and Tabaqui the jackal whined a greeting. The wolves did not like him, because he ran errands for the tiger and carried tales from den to den.
Tabaqui sat down and cracked a dry bone with great pleasure. Then he told the wolves that Shere Khan, the great tiger, had moved his hunting ground to these very hills.

Father Wolf said that Shere Khan had no right to move his hunting ground without giving fair warning. He also said that the tiger was lame in one foot, and that he killed cattle because he could not catch quicker game.

Suddenly a loud, angry whine rolled up from the valley below, and every animal on the hillside fell silent. Tabaqui grinned, for he knew that this was the cry of Shere Khan, who had missed his supper.
Father Wolf heard a rustle in the bushes and sprang, but he stopped in the air. In front of him was a naked human baby, no bigger than a puppy, and it looked up and laughed.
Mother Wolf told her husband to bring the child inside, so that she could look at him properly. The baby crawled in among the cubs, pressed against her warm side and was not afraid at all.
Mother Wolf said that the man's cub was hers now, and she would raise him among her own cubs. She called him Mowgli, which means the Frog, because he was bare and smooth.
Suddenly the moonlight vanished, for the huge head and shoulders of Shere Khan were blocking the cave mouth. His voice came in, deep and angry, and Tabaqui, who was behind him, gave a cry of joy.
Shere Khan said that a man's cub had run this way, and that its parents had gone. Mother Wolf answered that the cub was hers, and that no striped cattle-killer would take it.
The cave was too narrow for the tiger's great shoulders, and he could not get in. He roared that the Pack would decide, and that he would come back for the cub.

Father Wolf said that the Law was clear, because a cub must be shown to the Pack before it can be accepted. So the family set out under the moon, and he carried the baby in his mouth as gently as a cub.
Many wolves had already come to the Council Rock, young and old, grey and black. Akela, the great lone wolf who led them, lay at full length on his stone above the crowd.
The man's cub sat up and began to play with some pebbles that glittered in the moonlight. He did not seem afraid of the wolves, who stared at him in silence.
Akela raised his head and called the old words that opened every meeting, asking the wolves to look well. Then a deep voice rose from the shadows, for Shere Khan had come to claim his prize.
Akela said that the Law was older than the tiger, and that a cub might be saved if two wolves spoke for him. They could not be his father or mother, and nobody moved.
Then a heavy brown shape rose from the edge of the circle, and the wolves saw Baloo, the sleepy old bear. He taught them the Law, and he said that the man's cub did no harm.

A soft voice said that it was a shame to kill a naked cub, and Bagheera the black panther glided into the ring. He offered a fat young bull, killed that very evening, as the price of the child's life.
The hungry wolves growled their agreement, and Akela said that the cub would stay. Shere Khan stalked away into the night, snarling that he would be back.
The years went by, and Mowgli grew up with his wolf brothers in the cave on the hill. He ate what they ate, played what they played and never knew that he was different.
Father Wolf taught Mowgli to understand the jungle, one noise at a time. Every rustle in the grass and every splash in the pool had a meaning, and Mowgli learned them all.
Gray Brother, the eldest of the cubs, was Mowgli's closest friend, and they were seldom apart. Together they climbed trees for fruit, swam in the river and raced through the long grass.
Baloo, the old brown bear, was Mowgli's teacher, and he taught him the Law of the Jungle. When Mowgli forgot a word, Baloo gave him a cuff, and Mowgli was often cross about it.
Baloo also taught Mowgli the Master-Words, a different greeting for each of the jungle peoples. The most important one meant, “We be of one blood, ye and I.”
Bagheera, the black panther, often lay on a branch above the lessons and watched with half-closed eyes. He was gentler than Baloo, and Mowgli was fonder of him than he liked to say.
One day Bagheera showed Mowgli a bare patch under his throat, where a collar had once been. He had been born in a king's cage at Oodeypore, and he knew the ways of men.
Bagheera told Mowgli that he had been saved by a bull, and that a price had been paid for his life. He said that Shere Khan had not forgotten the man-cub, and that the tiger was waiting.

Baloo said that the Monkey People, the Bandar-log, were not to be trusted, for they had no Law, no leader and no memory. They talked and chattered and made big plans, but they forgot everything by the next day.
Mowgli grew tired of so many lessons, and one afternoon he said so rudely. Baloo cuffed him hard, and the boy ran off angrily, because he had never been hit like that.
Mowgli found a quiet glade and sat down by himself, still angry. To take his mind off his troubles, he began to weave branches and vines into a little shelter.
There was a rustle overhead, and a crowd of grey monkeys appeared on the branches. Mowgli remembered Baloo's warning, but the monkeys looked so friendly that he did not run away.
The monkeys shouted that they were great, free and wonderful, and they told Mowgli that he must join them. They had never seen anyone weave so well, and they said that they wanted to learn.
Without warning, a dozen small hands grabbed Mowgli by the arms and legs and lifted him off the ground. Before he could shout, he was being carried up into the branches.
The monkeys leapt from tree to tree with Mowgli in their arms, faster than any wolf could run. He felt sick and dizzy, because the ground was a long way below, and he could hardly breathe.
Looking up through the leaves, Mowgli saw a great bird circling in the sky. It was Chil the kite, and Mowgli remembered that Baloo had taught him a Master-Word for the kites.
Mowgli cried out the Master-Word, “We be of one blood, ye and I,” and begged Chil to mark the way. The kite turned his great head and, to Mowgli's joy, answered that he had heard.

Chil flew across the hills, searching until he found Baloo, who had been calling for the boy, and Bagheera, who was searching beside him. He told them that the monkeys had carried Mowgli off toward the Cold Lairs.
Baloo hung his head, for he knew that his hard cuffs had sent the boy into danger. Bagheera was furious, but he knew that the two of them could not fight so many monkeys by themselves.
Bagheera said that there was only one creature that the monkeys feared, and that was Kaa the rock python. Baloo shivered, for Kaa was a dangerous friend, but he agreed that there was no other way.
As they ran across the hills, Bagheera told Baloo what he knew of Kaa. The python was patient, strong and as long as a tree, and he was always hungry.
At last they found Kaa lying on a warm rock in the sun, looking at himself. He had just shed his old skin, and his new coat shone in gold and brown.

Bagheera bowed low and gave the hunting greeting, for Kaa was proud and quick to take offence. He whispered to Baloo that they must be very polite, because a python who has just changed his skin is hungry.

Bagheera praised the new skin, saying that it was the finest in the jungle, and Kaa was pleased at once. He asked in his soft, hissing voice what the bear and the panther wanted from a lonely old snake.

Baloo and Bagheera explained that the Bandar-log had stolen the man-cub, whom Baloo taught and Bagheera loved. At the name of the monkeys, Kaa's body stiffened, and he hissed with a sound like wind in dry grass.
Kaa said that the monkeys had called him a yellow earth-worm and said that he had lost his teeth. He promised that he would be glad to teach them a lesson.
Kaa asked what kind of cub the boy was, and Baloo told him that Mowgli was brave and spoke the Master-Words. When he heard this, Kaa said that the boy was a friend of the jungle and must be saved.

As the sun went down, the three of them set out, with Chil the kite circling above to show the way. They crossed a river, a long marsh and a stony ridge without stopping, and Kaa glided as fast as the others could run.
Late in the night they came to a hill covered with old trees, and there, through the leaves, they saw high stone walls. It was the Cold Lairs, the ruined city that a king had built long ago.
Kaa told Bagheera and Baloo to run on ahead and fight the monkeys, so that the Bandar-log would not look for him. He would come slowly by another way, for a python is not made to hurry over stones.
Meanwhile the monkeys had brought Mowgli into the Cold Lairs, a city of broken walls and roofless houses. Trees grew out of the stone floors, and fig roots had split the old marble.
The monkeys crowded around Mowgli and boasted that they were wise, strong and clever, and that they had a fine new teacher. Mowgli was tired, hungry and thirsty, and nobody offered him anything.
The monkeys began a plan to build a great house, but they forgot it in a minute and started something else. Mowgli saw that Baloo had been right, because they had no memory.
Mowgli tried to find a way out of the city, but the walls were high and the gates were blocked with fallen stone. Whenever he moved too far, the monkeys pulled him back and told him to stay.
The evening passed, and the stars came out over the ruined towers. Mowgli believed that Chil had carried his message, and he was sure that Baloo and Bagheera were already on their way.
Suddenly there was a roar, and Bagheera sprang over the wall into the middle of the monkeys. He struck right and left, but a hundred of the Bandar-log leapt on his back.

The monkeys piled on top of Bagheera, and he rolled over and over until he fell into the great water tank. There he could breathe at last, though the monkeys sat on the edge and threw stones at his head.
Baloo came running after him, and for a time the old bear held back the crowd with his heavy paws. But the monkeys were too many, and soon he was buried too.

While the fight went on, a group of monkeys seized Mowgli and pushed him into a small summer-house with no roof. They shut him in behind a screen of stone, and there he could only look out through the cracks.
Through a crack in the stone Mowgli saw only a heaving mass of monkeys, and he could not tell whether his friends were alive. Then, very faintly, he heard a long, dry hiss from beyond the wall.

A long shadow slid along the top of the broken wall, and the nearest monkeys stopped shouting, one after another. Kaa had come by his quiet road at last, and no monkey had seen him until he was there.
Kaa went straight to the summer-house and struck its wall with his great flat head, again and again. At the third blow the marble cracked, and a piece the size of a door crashed down.
Mowgli gave the Master-Word for the snakes, and Kaa answered in his soft voice that he had come as a friend. He told the boy to keep out of the way, because there was hunting to be done.
Kaa raised his head and began a strange, slow dance. He swayed from side to side and wove great figures in the air, and the moonlight shone on his new skin.
The monkeys stood still and stared, for nobody who watches the Dance of Hunger can look away. Their mouths hung open, their eyes grew round, and they began to shuffle slowly nearer.
Then Mowgli saw something dreadful, for Bagheera had climbed out of the tank and Baloo had struggled up from the ground. Like the monkeys, both of them were walking slowly toward Kaa.
Mowgli ran forward and seized Baloo by the shoulder and Bagheera by the ear, and pulled with all his strength. They were heavy and slow, but they began to stumble backward, away from the circle.
Bagheera said that Mowgli had saved the bear and the panther from the Dance of Hunger. The two of them hung their heads, for such a thing was hard for proud hunters to admit.

Then Kaa took his meal, as a hungry snake must, and the monkeys who had been under his spell were never seen again. The rest of the Bandar-log fled in terror, screaming through the dark until the city was empty.

At dawn, Mowgli thanked Kaa with the Master-Word, and the python lowered his head and said that the debt was paid. Then the boy and his two friends walked out of the silent city and set off for the jungle.

When Mowgli came home, Mother Wolf scolded him for staying away so long and then held him close without saying anything more. Baloo, still ashamed of his temper, promised that he would never raise his paw to the boy again.

The years passed, and Mowgli grew tall and strong, until he could outrun most of the young wolves. He found that he could stare into a wolf's eyes until the wolf looked away, and he laughed at it, for it was a game.
One evening Gray Brother came to Mowgli in secret and warned him about Shere Khan. The tiger was whispering to the young wolves, and he said that a man's cub had no place in the Pack.
Bagheera said that Gray Brother was right, and that Akela was growing old and slow. When the old leader missed his kill, the young wolves would turn against him, and against Mowgli too.
Bagheera said that Mowgli would need a weapon that the tiger feared. The jungle called it the Red Flower, and it was kept by men in the village.
Mowgli had a human face, and he was not afraid of the village. He said that he would fetch the Red Flower that night, and feed it with sticks as he had seen the villagers do.

That night Mowgli ran through the dark forest until he came to the edge of a village. He crouched behind a bush and watched the huts, where lamps were glowing and people were eating their evening meal.
At the door of one hut there stood an earthen pot full of glowing coals, which someone had put out for the night. Mowgli lifted it, burned his fingers a little and ran away with it.

As he ran home through the jungle, Mowgli fed the fire with dry sticks and bark, just as he had seen the wood-cutters do. The Red Flower grew bright and warm, and it did not hurt him if he was careful.

Bagheera was waiting on a flat rock, and his eyes grew wide when he saw the pot in Mowgli's hands. He said that Mowgli had done what no animal in the jungle would ever dare, and that the Red Flower would be his weapon.
One night the Pack was hunting a buck, and Akela, as leader, made the first jump. He was a moment too slow, the buck leapt aside, and the old wolf fell short on the grass.
Akela lay alone on his rock, for he knew what the Law said about a leader who missed his kill. In the shadows, Shere Khan was whispering busily to the young wolves.
When the Council met, the wolves sat in a ring around the great rock, and Shere Khan lay among the young ones. Akela stood in front of them, tired but proud, and began to speak.
Akela said that he had led the Pack for many years without failing, and that no wolf had ever lost a fight with a stranger. If they wanted him dead, they must come one by one and fight him fairly.

Shere Khan said that there was no need to waste time on a toothless old wolf who was already finished. The real question was the man-cub, who belonged to the tiger by right, and he asked the Pack to give him up.
Suddenly the wolves saw a light moving among the trees, and Mowgli stepped into the ring with a burning branch in his hand. The Red Flower scared them, and they drew back with wide eyes.
Mowgli said that Shere Khan had called him a man, and so he would act like one. He beat the tiger across the face with the burning branch until the great cat howled and ran out of the circle.
Then Mowgli stood in front of Akela and told the wolves that nobody would hurt him while the Red Flower burned. He said that they were ungrateful, and they hung their heads.

Mowgli had decided that he could not stay with a Pack that had turned against him. For the first time in his life he wept, and he asked Mother Wolf whether he was dying, because he had never felt tears.
Mowgli said goodbye to Father Wolf, Mother Wolf and Gray Brother, who promised that he would visit. He swore that he would come back one day and lay Shere Khan's skin on the Council Rock.
In India, the summer rains came down in a flood, and a young mongoose called Rikki-Tikki-Tavi was washed out of his burrow. He held on to a tuft of grass as the water carried him away.
A small English boy named Teddy found the wet little animal lying on the path. He thought that it was dead, and he said that they should have a funeral.
Teddy's father picked him up and said that he was not dead, but only half drowned. They dried him with a cloth and wrapped him in cotton wool by the fire.
Rikki-Tikki was not afraid of people, because his family had a rule, which was to run and find out. After a breakfast of fruit and egg, he sat on Teddy's shoulder, feeling at home.
Rikki-Tikki spent the day exploring the whole bungalow, from the writing desk to the bathroom. He put his nose into a bottle of ink and sat on Teddy's father's lap while he wrote.
Teddy's mother was afraid that a wild animal might bite the boy in the night. Her husband said that Rikki-Tikki would be a better guard than any dog, because he hated snakes.
The garden was a large one, full of rose bushes, lemon trees and clumps of bamboo. Rikki-Tikki's eyes shone, for it was just the kind of place where a young hunter could find something to do.
In a bush he found Darzee the tailorbird and his wife, who were crying beside their nest of sewn leaves. One of their babies had fallen out of the nest the day before, and a snake had eaten it.
Darzee said that two great cobras, Nag and his wife Nagaina, lived in the garden. They hunted wherever they liked, and no bird or beast could stop them.
Suddenly the grass moved, and the great cobra Nag rose up out of it with his hood spread wide. Rikki-Tikki's fur bristled, but he stood still, and Darzee shrieked a warning.

At Darzee's cry Rikki-Tikki jumped straight up into the air, and Nagaina's strike hit only the empty path. Both cobras slid away into the long grass, and Rikki-Tikki understood that he had made two enemies.
The next day Teddy was playing on the gravel path when Rikki-Tikki saw a tiny brown snake creeping toward his hand. It was a Karait, which is small but as deadly as any cobra.
Rikki-Tikki leapt on the Karait and fought it in a swirl of dust until it was dead. Teddy's mother hugged her son, and she said that the mongoose had saved his life.

That night, as Rikki-Tikki explored the dark house, he met Chuchundra the muskrat, a miserable creature who crept along the wall. He had never once crossed the middle of the floor, because he was always afraid.

Chuchundra begged Rikki-Tikki not to tell Nag that he had spoken, and then he whispered that Nag was in the garden. The cobra would come into the bungalow that night, and his voice shook so much that Rikki-Tikki could hardly hear.
Rikki-Tikki hurried to the bathroom, which was dark and cool, and hid behind the big water jar. He kept very still and watched the little hole in the wall where the bath water ran out.
At last a long black shape slid out of the drain, and Nag coiled himself around the water jar. He told his wife that when the people were gone, the garden would be theirs.

Rikki-Tikki leapt out and fastened his teeth in the back of Nag's head and held on, whatever happened. The great snake thrashed about the room and whipped him against the walls, the floor and the water jar.
The noise woke the house, and Teddy's father ran in with a gun in his hand. He fired once, and Nag fell dead on the floor while Rikki-Tikki lay beside him, tired and sore.
Teddy's mother put Rikki-Tikki on the bed beside her son and thanked him. In the morning Darzee sang a song to say that Nag was dead, but the little mongoose knew that Nagaina was alive.
Rikki-Tikki told Darzee that it was no time for singing. Nagaina was still alive, and she would be furious about her husband.

Rikki-Tikki asked Darzee where Nagaina kept her eggs, and the bird thought for a moment. He said that they were hidden in the melon bed, at the end nearest the wall, where the sun shone nearly all day.
Darzee's wife was clever, and she offered to help. She fluttered across the grass in front of Nagaina, dragging one wing as if it were broken, and the angry cobra followed.
In the melon bed, under the leaves, Rikki-Tikki found the nest, with a heap of white eggs in the warm earth. He broke them all but one, and he kept that one safe in his mouth.

Darzee's wife screamed that Nagaina had given up the chase and had gone to the veranda, where the family was eating breakfast. Rikki-Tikki, with the egg in his mouth, sprinted after her through the flower beds.
When Rikki-Tikki reached the veranda, he saw Nagaina coiled on the matting beside Teddy's chair. The family sat frozen, for the cobra's head was only a few inches from the boy.

Rikki-Tikki called out to Nagaina that he had her last egg, and she turned her head away from Teddy at once. She hissed that he must give it back, and that she would go away and leave the garden forever.
Rikki-Tikki rolled the egg across the floor, and Nagaina snatched it in her mouth. Teddy's father dragged the boy out of reach, and Rikki-Tikki dashed after her down the garden path.
Nagaina raced for her hole under the thorn bush, and she went into it headfirst. Rikki-Tikki, without stopping to think, went in right behind her, into the dark.
After a long, terrible silence, Rikki-Tikki crawled out of the hole, dusty and tired but unhurt. He said that the widow would never come out again, and Darzee sang a joyful song.
High in the hills of India there was a camp where the Government kept its working elephants and the men who drove them. Among the huts and the tall trees, a small boy was growing up.
The boy's name was Little Toomai, and he was ten years old. His father, his grandfather and his great-grandfather had all driven elephants, and he meant to do the same.

Big Toomai's elephant was Kala Nag, which means Black Snake, and he was the largest and oldest in the camp. He had hauled guns and timber for many years, and he knew more about the work than most of the men.

Every morning Little Toomai washed Kala Nag in the river, scrubbing him with a stone while the elephant lay on his side. After the bath the boy fed him sugar-cane, and Kala Nag always lifted him gently to his neck.
The elephants of the camp were tied in long lines, one beside another, each with a rope around its foot. Among them was Pudmini, a gentle she-elephant, and every one of them knew Little Toomai.
Each season the men caught wild elephants by driving whole herds into a huge stockade, which was called the Keddah. Kala Nag and the other tame elephants helped with this dangerous work.
Little Toomai begged his father to let him come to the Keddah. Big Toomai only shook his head and said that a boy of ten was too young, and that he must wait.
One day Petersen Sahib, the white officer who was in charge of all the elephant catching, came to look at the lines. He saw Little Toomai standing beside Kala Nag, and he smiled.
Machua Appa told Petersen Sahib that the boy wished to be an elephant catcher. The officer laughed kindly, and said that Little Toomai could join the hunt when he had seen the elephants dance.
Little Toomai asked the old drivers where the elephants danced, and every man in the camp laughed at him. They said that nobody had ever seen it, and that it was only a story to tell by the fire.
That evening the drivers sat around the camp fire and ate their rice, while the elephants stood in the dark behind them. Little Toomai sat close to his father and listened to the old men talk.
An old driver began to speak of the dance of the wild elephants, which was a secret of the deep jungle. He said that on certain nights they gathered in a hidden place and danced in the moonlight.
The old man said that the dancing ground was a bare place on a hill, packed as hard as stone. Nobody could say how many years the dance had gone on there.
Big Toomai laughed and said that no man had ever seen the dance, and that it was a tale for children. Little Toomai did not laugh, for he believed every word.
Later the boy went to Kala Nag's place and lay down on the straw beside him. The camp grew quiet, and he looked at the stars between the leaves.
Kala Nag did not lie down to sleep, as he did most nights. He stood with his head high and his huge ears spread wide, as if he were listening for a far-off sound.
From somewhere in the distant hills came a faint, low sound, like the beating of a heavy drum. Little Toomai sat up on his straw and held his breath to listen.
Kala Nag pulled at the heavy chain that held him to the peg, once, twice and a third time. The peg came out of the earth with a sound like a tooth being drawn.
Little Toomai jumped up, seized Kala Nag's ear, and scrambled onto his neck before he had time to be afraid. He knew that the old elephant meant to go to the hills, and he would not be left behind.
Kala Nag turned and walked out of the sleeping camp, as silently as a cloud, with the boy on his neck. Not one man heard them go, and soon the trees closed in around them.
The old elephant climbed steadily through the dark forest, brushing aside every branch that stood in his way. Little Toomai lay flat on his neck, and he could feel the great muscles moving under him.
After a time a second elephant stepped out of the shadows, a huge wild tusker with a dusty coat. He fell in beside Kala Nag without a sound, and then a third joined them.
More and more elephants came out of the jungle on every side, big and small, old and young. Before long, Little Toomai was riding in the middle of a great moving river of grey backs.

At last the herd climbed to the top of a long hill and stepped out of the trees into the moonlight. There in front of them lay a round clearing, bare and flat, where the ground was trodden as hard as stone.
The elephants gathered in the clearing, a great crowd of them, wild and tame together. Kala Nag took his place among them, and Little Toomai sat still and held his breath.
Then the dance began, slowly at first, with the whole herd rocking. The elephants rocked from side to side and stamped their enormous feet in time, and the whole hill seemed to shake.
