The elephants danced in great circles and stamped until the dust rose in clouds. Little Toomai felt the drumming in his bones, and his teeth rattled in his head.
The hours went by, and the moon sank slowly toward the hills. At last the stamping grew slower and softer, until it stopped, and the elephants stood still.
At dawn the herd drifted away into the jungle as quietly as it had come. Kala Nag carried the sleeping boy home along the path, and he stopped in his old place at the picket.

The drivers followed the broad trail through the forest and found the dancing ground, hard and bare, just as the boy had said. Petersen Sahib named him Toomai of the Elephants, and the whole camp cheered.

Mowgli walked across the hills all through the dawn, with the smoke of the village fires rising ahead of him. He had been born among men, but he had never lived with them, and he felt strange and shy.
When Mowgli reached the village, the people came out of their houses and stared at him. He was barefoot, with long black hair, and he could not understand a single word that they said.
Then a woman named Messua came out of a nearby hut and looked closely into his face. She cried out softly, for he reminded her of her little son, whom a tiger had carried off long ago.
Messua said that he must be hungry, and she took him into her house and gave him milk and bread. Mowgli did not understand her words, but he understood her kindness.
That night Mowgli lay on the floor of Messua's house, and the roof and the walls pressed in on him. He felt like an animal in a trap, and at last he went to sleep beside the open door.
Each day Messua taught Mowgli the names of the things in the house, and he learned fast. He had already learned the speech of every jungle people, and a new language did not frighten him.

The village boys laughed at the way Mowgli ate and walked, and he did not understand their jokes. But when they raced him along the dusty lane, he ran faster than any of them, and soon they stopped laughing.
In the evenings Buldeo, the old village hunter, told tales of the jungle by the fire. One of them was about a boy raised by wolves, and when Mowgli laughed at the story, the old man was very angry.
The headman said that a boy who ate the village's food must work for it, and he sent Mowgli to the buffaloes. Mowgli found that he liked it, for the great animals were calm and gentle.
At the head of the herd walked Rama, the greatest bull, who had horns as wide as a doorway. He looked at Mowgli for a long time, and then he lowered his head and followed where the boy led.
At noon the heat was so great that the buffaloes lay in the river up to their noses. The herd boys sat on their broad backs and dozed, and Mowgli watched the water slide past.
Mowgli grew fond of his herd, and he found that they understood him when he spoke. He had learned many animal languages, and the slow, deep speech of the buffaloes was an easy one.
One evening, as the herd was walking slowly home, a grey shape came out of the long grass at the edge of the field. It was Gray Brother, and he had come a long way to find his friend.
Gray Brother whispered that Shere Khan was not far away. The tiger had been hiding in the dry ravine near the village for many days, waiting for the boy to come out alone.
The ravine was a narrow valley with steep rocky walls, and there were only two ways out of it, the top and the bottom. Mowgli saw that anyone caught inside would be in a trap.
Mowgli told Gray Brother that the whole herd of buffaloes would be driven down the ravine. A tiger can fight many things, but he cannot fight a hundred angry bulls.
Gray Brother ran off through the dusk to find Akela, who lived far away in the Seeonee hills. Mowgli promised that he would meet them both the next morning at the head of the ravine.
That night Mowgli lay awake for a long time in Messua's house, thinking about the tiger and the Pack. His heart was quiet, because he knew exactly what he meant to do.
At dawn Mowgli led the whole herd out of the village, and the other herd boys wanted to come with him. He told them to stay behind, because it was his day to take the buffaloes out alone.
At the head of the ravine, Gray Brother and old Akela were waiting among the rocks. Akela bowed his grey head, and Mowgli laid his hand on it, remembering the Council Rock.
Mowgli rode Rama to the edge of the ravine and looked down into the shadows. Far below, half hidden among the rocks, lay a long striped shape, and it was Shere Khan.
Akela and Gray Brother cut the herd in two, as if they had done it all their lives. They drove one half around the hill toward the lower end of the ravine.
Mowgli sat on Rama and waited while the wolves took their places at the other end of the ravine. The sun climbed higher, and the bulls shifted and stamped, sensing that something was about to happen.
When the sun was high, Mowgli cupped his hands and called down into the ravine, using the tiger's name. He said that the man-cub whom Shere Khan had hunted so long was here, and ready.
The tiger rose to his feet with a growl, and he looked up at the boy on the bull. Then he looked down the valley, and his eyes widened, for he saw that he was caught.
Shere Khan sprang at the wall of the ravine and tried to climb it, but the rock was steep and smooth. His old lame foot slipped, and he slid back to the bottom, snarling.
Mowgli raised his arm and gave the herd the old call that he had taught them. Rama lowered his horns and leapt forward, and the bulls swept after him down the slope.
The herd thundered down the narrow valley like a wave of horns and dust, and the rocks shook beneath their feet. At the bottom, the other half of the herd came up to meet them.
Shere Khan was trapped between the two halves of the herd, with steep walls on either side. His long hunt for the man-cub ended there, and the old fear of the jungle was gone.
Mowgli rode down into the quiet ravine, where the herd was calm again, and stood beside the great body. He remembered his promise at the Council Rock, and he knew that it was time to keep it.
Mowgli took out his knife and began to skin the tiger, as the village men did with a deer. It was slow work, and the two wolves sat watching with grave eyes.
While Mowgli was working, there was a noise on the path above, and old Buldeo came puffing along with his long gun. He had come looking for the buffaloes, and he stopped when he saw the skin.
Buldeo said that the tiger had been his prey for years, and that the skin must be given to him. He knew that the Government paid a good reward for a dead tiger, and he wanted the money.
Mowgli answered that the skin was not for the Government or for Buldeo. He had promised it to the wolves of the Seeonee, and nobody else would have it.
Buldeo grew angry and raised his gun, but two grey wolves rose silently from the rocks behind him. He dropped the gun in terror, for he had never seen such wolves.
Buldeo turned and ran all the way back to the village, shouting that Mowgli was a sorcerer who spoke to wolves. He did not stop until he reached the headman's door.
Mowgli sighed, rolled up the skin, and drove the buffaloes back toward the village, for they belonged to the people there. He did not yet know what Buldeo had said about him.
When Mowgli reached the village, a crowd of angry men with sticks was waiting at the gate. They shouted that he was a sorcerer, and a wizard who made friends with wild animals.

The villagers closed their doors against him and began to throw stones, and one struck Mowgli on the shoulder. He could not understand why men would hurt someone who had done them no harm, and he walked on through the street.
Messua stood weeping in her doorway, but there was nothing she could do against the whole village. Mowgli looked at her kind face once, and then he walked away into the dusk.
Mowgli walked on through the dark fields until he came to the edge of the jungle. The old night smells of earth and leaves and water rose around him, and he felt at home.
Before long Akela and Gray Brother caught up with him among the trees, and they greeted him without any words. The three of them went on together toward the Seeonee hills as the moon rose.
At dawn they came to the cave on the hillside where Mowgli had been raised. Mother Wolf ran out and licked his face, and Father Wolf stood beside her with his tail wagging.

Mowgli sat at the mouth of the cave and told them about the buffaloes, the village and the death of Shere Khan. Mother Wolf said that she had always known he would keep his promise, and then the tired boy slept all day.

When the sun went down, Mowgli woke from a long sleep, walked to Council Rock and spread the tiger's skin on the great flat stone. He held down its edges with four heavy rocks, so that the wind could not move it.
Standing beside the skin, Mowgli gave the old call of the Seeonee Pack, the call that opens every council. The wolves came running from every part of the hills, until the rock was ringed with grey.
The wolves looked at the skin, and for a long moment nobody spoke. Then a great cry of welcome rose from the whole Pack, and Akela was the first to answer.
The wolves begged Mowgli to come back and lead them in the place of the aged Akela. Mowgli thanked them, but he said that he would rather be their brother than their master.
Mowgli stood on the skin and sang a song about the hunt, and Baloo and Bagheera came out of the trees to join the Pack. The wolves howled with joy until the hills rang with it.

From that day Mowgli ran with his wolf brothers through the moonlit forest, as happy as he had ever been. Shere Khan was gone, his friends were close, and the jungle that had raised him was his home again.

The seasons turned, and Mowgli grew up in the cave on the hill with Father Wolf, Mother Wolf and the four cubs who had become his brothers. He ate what they ate, quarrelled and played as they did, and never once suspected that a boy was any different from a wolf. The jungle gave him warmth, food and an endless playground, and for years he asked for nothing more.

Father Wolf took the boy out into the dusk and taught him the language of the jungle, one sound at a time. Every rustle in the grass, every flutter of wings in the branches and every splash in a pool meant something to those who listened carefully, and Mowgli learned to read them as another child would read his letters. By the end of the year he could tell a hunting owl from a harmless bat by the beat of its wings alone.

Of all the wolf cubs, Gray Brother, the eldest, was dearest to Mowgli, and the two of them were seldom out of each other's company. They climbed trees together to steal fruit, swam in the cool river as the sun climbed, and raced through the long grass until they dropped, gasping and laughing, in the shade. Even then, the wolves called Mowgli the Frog, and he was proud of the name.

Baloo, the sleepy old brown bear, was as good as his word and taught Mowgli the Law of the Jungle from morning to noon. He taught it with great patience and also, when the boy forgot a line, with a heavy paw that knocked him over, for Baloo said that a hard cuff was better than a quick death. Mowgli rubbed his ears and sulked about it for the rest of the afternoon, but he never stopped learning.

There were the Master-Words as well, a greeting for each of the jungle peoples, which a hunter might call out in danger and be spared. The kites had one, the snakes another, the bears and the wolves one more, and the strongest meant simply, “We be of one blood, ye and I.” Mowgli learned them all, and Baloo, who had little faith in the boy's memory, made him say them again at every sunset.

Bagheera, the sleek black panther, often lay along a high branch above the lessons with half-closed eyes, and every time Mowgli made a mistake, he purred like a cat that has eaten well. He was far less stern than Baloo, though he had little patience with foolishness, and Mowgli was fonder of him than he cared to admit. Between the bear and the panther, the boy was growing up with two friends who had little in common but love.

One afternoon Bagheera made Mowgli feel the bare patch of skin under his chin where a collar had once rubbed the fur away. Then Bagheera told him gravely how he had come to the Pack, bought for the price of a bull, and he reminded him that Shere Khan had sworn to return. Baloo sat up and told Mowgli firmly to keep away from the Bandar-log, the Monkey People, who lived in the trees and followed no Law. They had no leader, no memory and no honour, he said, and they talked a great deal about the noble things that they meant to do and then forgot them by the next sunrise. All the Jungle People despised them for it, and Baloo wished the boy to despise them too.

Mowgli sprang up with tears in his eyes and ran off into the trees, sore and ashamed.

Mowgli found a quiet glade where the sunlight fell in green patches, and he sat down alone, sore in his body and sorer in his pride. To forget his troubles he began to bend branches and twist vines into a little shelter, as he had once seen the villagers' children do, and the work soothed him. Soon he was humming to himself, and the forest around him seemed to hum along with him.

A rustle ran through the leaves above him, and a crowd of grey monkeys came swinging down to the nearest boughs, pulling faces, chattering and pointing at his work. Mowgli remembered Baloo's warning and knew that he ought to leave, but he was angry, lonely and far from home, and the monkeys seemed so cheerful. For a moment, in spite of everything that Baloo had told him, he almost wished to be liked.

The Bandar-log shouted in chorus that they were great, they were free, they were wonderful, and that every other beast in the jungle was jealous of them. In a few moments the boy, flattered and foolish, had begun to believe every word they said.

Without warning, a dozen small, strong hands seized Mowgli by the arms and legs, and he was hoisted into the air before he could cry out. The monkeys shrieked with joy, as if they had won a great prize, and in a flash the glade was empty, the shelter lay trampled on the ground, and the boy was swinging through the leaves. Far below him the earth rushed past like a green river, and the sun flashed between the leaves.

The Monkey People leapt from tree to tree with their burden, taking jumps that would have seemed impossible to any creature without wings, while the branches whipped Mowgli's face and the jungle floor flickered far below. He felt sick and dizzy, and all he could think of was that Baloo had been right, and that nobody in the forest knew where he was. Yet he had learned his lessons well enough, with Baloo's cuffs and Bagheera's purring, to stay calm and watch.

When he dared to look up through the leaves, Mowgli saw a great bird wheeling in the bright sky, with wings spread wide and eyes that missed nothing on the earth below. It was Chil the kite, and with a leap of hope he remembered that Baloo had taught him the Master-Word for the kite people. If it still worked, there was one creature in the jungle who could carry his message across the hills.

Mowgli cried out the Master-Word for the kites as loudly as the rushing wind allowed, and he begged Chil to mark the monkeys' trail and to tell Baloo and Bagheera where they were taking him. To his relief the great bird tilted his wings, answered in a thin whistle that the message would be carried, and swung away across the sky. Mowgli had never been so glad of a bear's cuffs, for it was Baloo's cuffs that had taught him the word.

He told them that the Bandar-log had carried the man-cub off through the tops of the trees, northward toward the Cold Lairs, and he repeated that the boy had called him brother. Then he rose up again into the sunshine, circling above the hills to watch how the chase would go.

Baloo hung his great head, for he knew that his hard hand had driven the boy out into the forest, and for once he had nothing to say. Bagheera was too anxious to be cruel, but he told his old friend that the Monkey People were too many and too quick for a bear and a panther, and that anger would not bring the boy back. After a moment Bagheera said, slowly, that there was only one creature in all the jungle whom the Bandar-log feared, and that was Kaa the great rock python, who loved to hunt them in the trees. Baloo shivered, because Kaa was a dangerous friend with a very long memory and a cold, strange appetite, yet he nodded and said that there was no other way. Together they turned and set off at a run through the long shadows to find him.

As they hurried over the hot rocks, Bagheera reminded Baloo of everything he knew about Kaa, the great rock python, who was as long as a tree, as patient as a hill and as strong as a flood. At last they found Kaa stretched out upon a sun-baked ledge of rock, turning his great flat head from side to side to admire himself. He had just shed his old skin, and the new one, patterned in brown and yellow, gleamed like polished wood in the evening light. The old python was so busy with his own beauty that he did not notice the two visitors at all.

Bagheera bowed his glossy head as low as it would go and gave the hunting greeting, for Kaa was proud, nearly blind until his new eyes had cleared, and quick to take offence at a bad word. Baloo copied him, though he found it hard to bend, and the two of them waited with great courtesy while Kaa turned his flat head slowly toward the sound. Every muscle of the huge snake rippled like water over smooth stones, and his coils shone in the sun.

Kaa said in a low hiss that the Bandar-log had called him a footless, yellow earth-worm, and that they had sworn he had lost every tooth in his head, which made him angrier than any hunter's spear could have done. His small, jewelled eyes glittered coldly, and the tip of his tail twitched from side to side.

As the sun sank, the three hunters set out together, with Chil the kite wheeling overhead in the failing light to show the road.
