Late in the night they climbed a wooded hill, and through the trees they saw the grey outline of high walls, broken towers and a great ruined palace. This was the Cold Lairs, the lost city that a king had built long before anyone could remember, and which the jungle was slowly taking back. A cloud of monkeys' voices, shrill and silly, drifted up to them on the night air.

Kaa told the others to run ahead and make as much noise as they could, so that the monkeys would be busy fighting them and would never think to look for a long yellow worm. He would come by another way, slowly and silently, because a python does not hurry over stones and has no wish to be seen. Baloo gave a deep sigh and Bagheera shook his head, but in the end they both obeyed him.

Meanwhile the Bandar-log had brought their captive into the Cold Lairs, a deserted city of roofless houses, crumbling towers and courtyards where fig trees had split the marble with their roots. A king had built it long ago and called it a wonder, but the jungle had taken it back, and now only monkeys lived among its broken stones. Mowgli was dropped in a courtyard, where he stared about him with wide and wondering eyes.

The monkeys crowded around Mowgli, shouting to each other that they were wise, strong and clever, and that no other tribe in the jungle had ever thought of taking a man-cub for a teacher. Nobody offered the boy a single nut, though he had not eaten since the morning, and the noise of fifty voices speaking at once made his head ache. He felt, in a way he had never done before, how very far from home he was.

Mowgli watched with growing amazement as the monkeys began a plan to weave great houses out of branches, forgot it within a minute and started instead to chase one another around the broken fountain. No monkey seemed to remember what any other had said, nor did any of them remember what he had meant to do himself. Baloo had been right about them in every word, and Mowgli wished that he had listened.

Mowgli began to look for a way out of the ruined city, walking along the edge of a terrace and peering through cracks in the stonework. The walls were tall, the gates were blocked with fallen blocks of marble, and each time he strayed too far, a dozen small hands dragged him back with cries of delight. He sat down on a stone, put his chin in his hands and began to think very hard.

The evening faded, the first stars glittered over the broken towers, and a cold wind began to whisper through the empty streets. Mowgli clung to the hope that Chil had carried his message and that Baloo and Bagheera were already running through the night to find him, though he could not know how many hours it would take. Meanwhile he kept his back to a wall and his eyes on the monkeys.

Suddenly a roar split the night air, and Bagheera sprang over the wall into the very middle of the crowd, striking about him with his terrible paws and sending monkeys flying in all directions. But the Bandar-log, who feared nothing in numbers, shrieked and swarmed over his back in hundreds, biting and tugging at his fur. Mowgli leapt up with a cry of joy that was lost in the noise.

The monkeys piled on top of Bagheera in a great grey mound of limbs and teeth, and he was driven backwards over the paving stones. At last he rolled into the old water tank at the edge of the courtyard, where the monkeys could not easily climb over him. He lay on the surface, panting, his black coat shining, while the Bandar-log danced on the bank and hurled bits of marble at his head.

Baloo came lumbering in behind his friend, and for a time the old bear cleared a ring around him with great sweeps of his heavy paws. He roared that he was the teacher of the Law and would have his pupil back, but the monkeys were as numerous as leaves. Gradually they overwhelmed him, until nothing could be seen of the bear but a heaving heap of grey bodies.

While the fight went on, a group of the monkeys seized Mowgli and bundled him into an old summer-house, a roofless marble pavilion with a lattice of stone across its windows. They pushed rubble against the door and left him inside with nothing to do but peer through the cracks at the struggle in the courtyard. Mowgli, who was no coward, hammered on the door and shouted that he was a wolf of the Seeonee Pack.

Through a crack in the stonework Mowgli saw only a heaving, screaming mass of monkeys where his friends had been, and he could not tell whether they were still alive. His heart sank, and he thought of Mother Wolf and Gray Brother and the green hills of home. Then, very faintly, from somewhere beyond the broken wall, there came a long, dry hiss like wind blowing through reeds.

A long shadow crept along the top of the broken wall, and the monkeys nearest to it stopped their shouting one after another and stared upward with open mouths. Kaa had come by his quiet road at last, and the Bandar-log, who had been too busy fighting to look behind them, saw him only when he was already above their heads. The silence that spread through the courtyard was like a cold wind blowing through an open window.

Kaa slid straight toward the little summer-house where Mowgli was shut, and he struck its marble wall with his flat, heavy head, drawing back and driving forward like a battering ram. At the third blow the old stone cracked from side to side, and at the sixth a section as large as a door crumbled and fell, leaving a gap through which the moonlight poured. Mowgli found himself looking up through the dust into a pair of glittering, unblinking eyes.

Mowgli gave the Master-Word of the snake people in a voice that shook only a little, and Kaa, with a nod of his enormous head, replied that he knew the boy for a friend. He told Mowgli to stay close to the broken wall, and to watch, and above all not to be afraid, because there was hunting to be done. Then he turned slowly around to face the Monkey People, who had begun to cry out in alarm.

Kaa raised the front part of his body high above the ground, and in the white light of the moon he began the slow, strange dance that was known as the Dance of Hunger. His great head swayed from side to side, drawing circles, then figures of eight, and then soft, shifting triangles, and the pattern of his new skin gleamed and flickered in the dark. His hissing, rising and falling in the quiet, was like a strange song without any words.

Not a monkey could take his eyes from the swaying snake, for no creature who has ever watched the Dance of Hunger can look anywhere else. The Bandar-log stood still, their mouths hanging open and their eyes growing wide and dull, and one by one they began to shuffle forward, like sleepwalkers, toward the circling head. Their chatter had died away completely, and the only noise was the whisper of Kaa's scales on the stone.

Then Mowgli saw something that made his blood run cold, for Bagheera had dragged himself out of the water tank and Baloo had struggled up from beneath the heap of monkeys. Both of them, with their eyes fixed on the snake, were walking slowly toward the dancing head, as helpless as the monkeys. Mowgli knew that he alone was not under the spell, because he was not looking at the dance.

Mowgli darted forward through the rows of dazed monkeys, seized Baloo by the shoulder and Bagheera by the ear, and pulled with all the strength of his young arms. They were heavy and slow, and they dragged against him like sleepers who do not wish to wake, but little by little they stumbled backward, away from the circle, until their eyes began to clear. Bagheera shook himself like a wet dog, and Baloo groaned and rubbed his face with both paws.

Bagheera looked down at the boy for a long moment and said, in an unsteady voice, that he and the bear owed their lives to a naked man-cub who had kept his head. Baloo, his fur still full of dust and torn leaves, hung his big head with shame, for it was hard for proud hunters to admit that they had walked into the jaws of a snake like frightened rabbits. Mowgli only laughed at their thanks, for he was very tired and wanted nothing but his bed.

Then Kaa took the meal that he had earned, quietly and without any cruelty, for hunger is the law of a python as it is of a wolf, and the monkeys who had watched his dance were never seen again. The rest of the Bandar-log fled in terror through the broken gates and over the walls, shrieking until the sound was lost among the trees. Soon there was no sound in the Cold Lairs but the whisper of the wind in the ruined courtyards.

When the grey light of dawn appeared above the towers, Mowgli stood before Kaa and thanked him once more with the Master-Word. The old python lowered his great head and said that the debt of the insults was paid, and that he now meant to sleep for a month. Then the boy, the bear and the panther walked out through the ruined gate into the cool morning, leaving the Cold Lairs as empty and still as it had been for a hundred years.

When Mowgli came limping home to the cave at last, Mother Wolf scolded him in a stream of angry words and then held him so close that he could hardly breathe. Baloo, who had followed him up the hill, said gruffly that he was sorry for his temper and that no cuff of his would ever again drive the boy into danger. After that, the old bear taught more gently, and Mowgli, who had never really minded the lessons, learned more quickly.

The years rolled by, and Mowgli grew tall and brown and strong, with muscles like cords, until there was scarcely a young wolf in the Pack who could outrun him over a long course. He discovered, too, that if he stared into a wolf's eyes for long enough, the animal would drop its own gaze in confusion, and he played at this for sport, never thinking that the wolves might resent it. Time, which seemed to move slowly for a boy, was moving very quickly for the Seeonee Pack.

One evening Gray Brother slipped through the grass and found Mowgli alone, and in a low voice he told him what the whole Pack was beginning to whisper. Shere Khan, he said, had been talking in the shadows to the young wolves, flattering them with tales of the good hunting that a tiger could give, and telling them that a man's cub did not belong. Mowgli sat very still while he listened, and the laugh went slowly out of his face.

Bagheera, who had heard it all before, told the boy softly that Gray Brother was right, and that the danger was greater than he knew. Akela, the great Lone Wolf, was growing old, and on the day that he failed to make his kill, the young wolves, who followed Shere Khan, would turn upon him and then upon the man-cub who defended him. It was only a matter of time, he said, and not much time, and the boy had better be ready.

Then Bagheera said that the only thing in the jungle that was stronger than all the claws of Shere Khan was a thing the Jungle People dared not name, and that Mowgli would have to fetch it for himself. The jungle called it the Red Flower, and it lived in the villages of men, in small pots of earth, for men alone knew how to keep it. Bagheera had seen it often through the bars of the King's cage, and he knew how much every beast feared it.

Mowgli listened with his chin in his hand, and when Bagheera had finished he said that he was not afraid of men, since he had a man's face himself, and that he would fetch the Red Flower that very night. He remembered seeing the wood-cutters feeding their fires with sticks and bark, and he thought that a thing so simple could not be as terrible as the Jungle People believed. Bagheera purred with satisfaction, and said that he had never for one moment doubted him.

That night Mowgli ran through the dark forest on his bare feet until he came to the edge of the fields, where the village of the men lay quiet under the stars. He crouched behind a bush, with the smell of smoke and cooking in his nose, and watched the mud huts, where yellow lamplight glowed and the people sat eating their evening meal. He had not seen human beings for many years, and his heart beat strangely.

At the doorway of one hut, Mowgli saw a pot of baked clay in which a bed of coals glowed red, waiting to be fed again in the morning. He lifted it gently, tasting the heat on his fingers and thinking that this was just a flower made of light, and then he slipped away between the fields before the sleepy dogs had time to bark. Not one person in the whole village noticed that the pot was missing from the doorway.

On the long way back through the jungle, Mowgli fed his Red Flower with dry sticks and strips of bark, blowing on it gently as he ran, and the coals brightened and sent up little tongues of yellow flame. He learned that it was a hungry thing, quick to bite if he was careless, but quick to grow if he was kind, and he found a strange new joy in carrying it. The night animals watched him go past with round, frightened eyes, and none of them dared to follow.

Bagheera was waiting on a flat rock at the edge of the hills, and when the boy appeared out of the trees, bearing his glowing pot like a lantern, the panther's green eyes opened wide. He said, in a voice that was almost a whisper, that Mowgli had done what no creature of the jungle had ever dared to do, and that the Red Flower would be his shield against the tiger. Mowgli sat up beside his secret fire all night, learning its moods, and he knew that his day of trial was coming.

One night the whole Pack ran down a young buck across a wide moonlit meadow, and Akela, as the leader, made the first spring that should have brought the animal down. But his legs were old and a little too slow, the buck swerved at the last moment, and the old wolf fell short on the grass with his empty jaws snapping on the air. It was a small mistake, but in the Pack it meant the end of his long rule.

Akela went back to his flat rock and lay there alone with his head upon his paws, for he knew perfectly well what the Law said about a leader who misses his kill. He did not ask for pity from anyone, and no wolf of the Pack was bold enough to offer any. In the darkness beyond the rock, Shere Khan moved quietly among the young wolves, murmuring and flattering and hinting that a new master would be welcome.

When the moon was high, the Pack gathered in a great ring around the Council Rock, and every face was turned toward Akela, who stood before them tired but still proud. Shere Khan lay at the edge of the circle among the young wolves, with Tabaqui at his feet and a wicked smile on his heavy face. Mowgli was not there, and nobody in the whole assembly could say where he had gone.

Akela said with dignity that he had led the Free People for many seasons without one of them losing a fight to a stranger, and that he now asked only for the right that the Law allowed him. Any wolf who wished to kill him must come forward and fight him fairly, one by one, as the Law of the Pack required. His voice was steady, and for a moment even the young wolves looked ashamed.

Shere Khan rose and rumbled that there was no sense in wasting time upon a toothless old fool who was finished already, and that the Pack had better settle the real question. The man-cub, he declared, had been kept too long by the Seeonee Pack, he was a danger to every wolf in the hills, and it was time that he was handed over. A growl went round the young wolves, and several of them said that the tiger was right.

Suddenly the wolves saw a light moving among the trees, and then Mowgli, tall and bare-limbed, strode into the circle with a blazing branch held high in his hand. He had lit it from the pot that he had kept hidden, and the red glow lit his face and the nervous eyes of the wolves, who fell back in alarm. There is nothing in the jungle that does not fear the Red Flower, and every one of them knew it.

Mowgli turned to Shere Khan and said that the tiger had called him a man-cub for years, and that he would now show him what a man could do. He swung the burning branch down upon the tiger's head and shoulders, again and again, until the whiskers crackled and the great cat, howling like a beaten cur, fled from the Council Rock with his tail between his legs. The wolves watched in silence, and not one of them dared to lift a paw to stop him.

Mowgli stepped in front of Akela and turned with the branch toward the ring, telling the young wolves that anyone who dared to lay a tooth on the old leader would answer to the Red Flower. He called them ungrateful dogs, who had forgotten every hunt that the old wolf had led, and for a long minute not one of them dared to meet his gaze. Then, one by one, with their heads hanging and their tails low, they turned and slunk away.

Mowgli had made up his mind that he could not stay with a Pack that had been so ready to turn against him, and the sorrow of it rose in him all at once. For the first time in his life, he wept, and the tears ran down his face, and he asked Mother Wolf in alarm whether he was dying, because he had never felt such a thing. She told him gently that these were called tears, which only the children of men are able to shed.

At dawn he said goodbye to Father Wolf and Mother Wolf, who licked his face and told him that the cave would always be his home, and to Gray Brother, who promised to come to him whenever he was needed. Mowgli swore that before the rains returned he would bring the skin of Shere Khan and lay it on the Council Rock. Then he turned toward the distant smoke of the village and walked away without looking back once.

In another part of India, during the heaviest rains of the summer, a flood washed a young mongoose called Rikki-Tikki-Tavi out of the burrow where he lived with his mother. The brown water carried him helplessly down a roadside ditch, spinning him round and round, until he caught a floating tuft of grass and clung to it with every claw. At last the current threw him up on a garden path, half drowned and weak as a kitten.

The garden belonged to a big bungalow, and as Rikki-Tikki lay in the sun with his eyes closed and his fur plastered flat, a small English boy called Teddy came out and found him. The boy declared that the creature was dead, and that they ought to bury it with a proper funeral, while his parents came out from the house to see what he had found. Rikki-Tikki, who was quite alive and growing more comfortable every minute, did not have the strength to object.

Teddy's father picked up the limp little body and discovered that it was still breathing, and that there was a good deal of life left in it. They dried him with a cloth, wrapped him in cotton wool and set him down in a warm place, and presently the mongoose sneezed, opened his eyes and tried to look dignified. Teddy was delighted, and his mother was not at all sure that she approved.

Rikki-Tikki had no fear of people, for his mother had taught him that the motto of all the mongoose family was “Run and find out,” and he wished to explore everything. After a breakfast of banana and boiled egg, he climbed up Teddy's arm and settled on his shoulder, as though he had lived in the bungalow for years. The boy laughed with pleasure, and the mongoose rubbed his small cold nose against his ear.

All that morning Rikki-Tikki hurried through the bungalow, climbing on tables, sniffing at lamps and running in and out of every room, because a mongoose can hardly bear a closed door. He dipped his nose into the ink on Teddy's father's desk, scampered along the edge of the bathtub and sat with great seriousness on the page that the man was writing. By the time the lamps were lit, the house had no more secrets from him.

Teddy's mother, who loved her son, was afraid that a wild creature might bite him in his sleep, and she said so in a worried voice. Her husband only laughed and replied that a tame mongoose was safer than a watchdog, because there are always snakes in an Indian garden, and a mongoose lives to fight them. He assured her that Rikki-Tikki would guard Teddy better than any man could do it.

The garden that surrounded the bungalow was only half-tamed, with rose bushes growing wild, lemon and orange trees weighed down with fruit and thick clumps of bamboo that rattled in the breeze. Rikki-Tikki's eyes shone as he stepped out on the path, for here was a place where a young hunter could roam for years, and the long grass was full of rustling. The old motto of his family had never seemed so fitting as it did on that bright morning.

In a thick bush beside the path Rikki-Tikki met Darzee, the tailorbird, who was sitting with his wife beside a nest that they had stitched together out of two big leaves. Both birds were crying bitterly, because one of their babies had tumbled out the day before, and Nag the cobra had eaten him. Rikki-Tikki, who did not like to see anyone in distress, asked politely whether he could help.

Darzee told him in a shaking voice that two great black cobras, Nag and his wife Nagaina, lived in the garden and hunted wherever they pleased among its birds, frogs and mice. Nobody could stop them, he said, and Rikki-Tikki was a fine fellow, but no mongoose of his size had ever fought a cobra. Rikki-Tikki felt his fur bristle, but he said that he was ready to try.

Suddenly there was a hiss in the grass, and a big black cobra rose slowly out of the green blades until his flat hood, marked with the sign of a spectacle, spread wide above Rikki-Tikki's head. Nag's cold eyes glittered, and he asked in a soft voice whether it was right for a mongoose to eat eggs, while his wife crept up behind through the grass. Rikki-Tikki's heart beat fast, but he did not move, and he did not look away.

At Darzee's frantic cry Rikki-Tikki sprang straight up into the air, and the cobra's head struck the dust where his back had been a moment before. She whipped round in fury, but the little mongoose had already turned, his fur like a bottle brush, and both snakes, deciding that they were not yet ready for a long fight, slid away into the long grass. Rikki-Tikki understood that he now had two deadly enemies in the garden, and that this was only the beginning.

Next day, while Teddy sat playing in the gravel of the garden path, Rikki-Tikki noticed a small, dusty brown snake wriggling through the dry grass toward the boy's outstretched hand. It was a Karait, an ugly little creature that is smaller than a worm but whose bite is as deadly as any cobra's. The boy, who was absorbed in his game, had no idea that anything dangerous was near him.

Rikki-Tikki flew at the Karait with a short, shrill cry, dodged its strike by a hair, seized it behind the head and held on until the fight was finished and the dusty little body lay still. Teddy's mother came running and snatched up her son, and she said, with tears in her eyes, that the mongoose had saved his life, while the father stroked Rikki-Tikki's back and pronounced him a hero. The mongoose, a little puzzled, thought it was a very small fuss for a simple day's work.

That night, while the family slept, Rikki-Tikki prowled through the bungalow and met Chuchundra, the muskrat, who crept along the skirting of the walls with his little head down, whimpering to himself. He was a miserable, timid creature who had never in his life dared to run across the middle of a room, and he was, therefore, almost always in tears. Rikki-Tikki, who was always cheerful and never once afraid, found him very odd indeed.

Chuchundra begged him not to say anything to Nag, because the cobra could hear a whisper through any wall, and then, in a voice that was barely a breath, he told Rikki-Tikki what he had overheard in the garden. Nag and Nagaina meant to creep in through the bathroom drain, he said, and they were waiting only for the people to fall asleep. Rikki-Tikki's whiskers twitched, and he thanked the muskrat for his news and went quietly away.

Rikki-Tikki hurried to the bathroom, where it was cool and still, and tucked himself behind the great earthenware water jar that stood in the corner. From there he watched the little hole in the wall through which the bath water ran out, and he reminded himself of what his mother had told him about waiting patiently for an enemy. He did not move a whisker, and the long minutes crawled by one after another.

At last there was a scrape in the dark, and a long black shape slid out of the drain and wound itself around the base of the great jar, within a foot of where Rikki-Tikki crouched. Nag whispered to his wife, in a voice like dry leaves, that when the man was dead and the woman gone, the people would leave the bungalow and the garden would be theirs again. Rikki-Tikki, hardly daring to breathe, thought that this was the moment he had been waiting for.

Rikki-Tikki sprang out of the shadows and sank his teeth in the back of Nag's head, close below the hood, and he held on with a grip that nothing could break. The huge cobra thrashed and whipped about the bathroom, dragging the little mongoose across the floor, up the wall and against the big jar, until the room rang and Rikki-Tikki was dizzy and bruised. Yet he did not let go, for a mongoose who loosens his bite is lost.

The crash of the struggle woke the whole bungalow, and Teddy's father ran into the bathroom in his nightclothes with a gun in his hands. He saw the mongoose clinging to the cobra's head, and without hesitation he fired, and the great snake fell and lay still upon the floor of the bathroom. Rikki-Tikki lay panting beside him, with his teeth still clenched in Nag's neck and his back aching from the blows.

Teddy's mother carried the exhausted mongoose off to bed and tucked him beside her sleeping son, and she thanked him with a kiss between the ears. In the morning, Darzee sat in the bush and sang a loud, proud song to say that the wicked Nag was dead, and that the garden was free from his shadow. But Rikki-Tikki, who knew a good deal about cobras, remembered Nagaina and her eggs and did not feel like singing.

Rikki-Tikki ran up to the bush and told the singing bird sharply that this was no time for a song, because Nag might be dead, but Nagaina was alive and angrier than ever. Darzee stopped in the middle of a note and looked ashamed, for he had thought only of his own safety. He said that Nagaina was sitting on the rubbish heap behind the stable, mourning for her husband.

Rikki-Tikki, who was thinking hard, asked Darzee where Nagaina kept her eggs, since a mother cobra would defend them more fiercely than her own life. Darzee said that they lay hidden in the melon bed, at the end nearest the wall, where the sun shone for the better part of the day. He added that it had not occurred to him to tell anyone, because the eggs seemed so unimportant at the time.

Darzee's wife, who was a good deal more clever than her husband, offered to lead Nagaina away, and she fluttered across the grass right in front of the cobra, dragging one wing as though it were broken. The furious snake, who thought that she was close to catching a helpless bird, chased her step by step across the garden. Meanwhile, Rikki-Tikki ran like the wind toward the melon bed, and he did not look back.

In the warmest corner of the melon bed, hidden beneath broad leaves, Rikki-Tikki found the nest, a heap of white eggs that were wrapped in soft skin rather than a hard shell. He knew that every one of them would hatch a young cobra, and one by one he broke them, but the very last one he took carefully in his mouth, because he thought that it might be useful. Then he heard Darzee's wife screaming in the distance, and he lifted his head to listen.

The bird's frightened voice came flying through the garden to tell Rikki-Tikki that Nagaina had given up the chase and gone straight to the veranda, where the family was sitting down to breakfast. Rikki-Tikki, with the egg held safe in his mouth, tore across the flower beds and under the rose bushes with his short legs flying. He knew that if he failed now, the one thing in the garden that Nagaina wanted would be Teddy's life.

When Rikki-Tikki reached the veranda, he saw a horrible sight, for Nagaina had coiled herself on the matting beside Teddy's chair, with her hood spread wide and her head swaying only a few inches from the boy's arm. Teddy's father and mother sat as stiff as stones, white-faced, knowing that the slightest movement would bring the cobra's strike. Rikki-Tikki, who had run so far and so fast, could scarcely breathe, and his legs shook.

Rikki-Tikki called out boldly to Nagaina and held up the last egg of her nest for her to see, and at the sight the cobra's whole body quivered and she turned her eyes from Teddy for the first time. She hissed that she must have it, and that if he gave it back, she would leave the garden and never trouble the family again. But Rikki-Tikki knew perfectly well that she did not mean a word of it.

Rikki-Tikki rolled the egg slowly across the matting, and at the moment when Nagaina darted her head to snatch it up, Teddy's father seized his son and dragged him out of danger. The cobra, with the egg in her jaws, shot off the veranda and across the lawn like a streak of black light, and Rikki-Tikki flew at her heels, snapping at her tail. Over the grass and between the roses the chase swept, with Darzee calling encouragement from a bush.

Nagaina raced toward her old rat hole under the thorn bush at the end of the garden, and slid into it, still gripping the last egg. Rikki-Tikki, who knew that this was the most dangerous moment of his life, took a deep breath and dived into the darkness after her, because a mongoose who follows a snake into her hole has no time to think. Darzee sat on a branch overhead and waited, his small heart pounding against his feathers.

After a long and terrible silence in which no sound came out of the hole, the earth near the entrance trembled, and Rikki-Tikki crawled out, dusty and weary but still alive. He said quietly that it was all over, and that the widow would never come out again, and the tailorbird above him burst into a glorious song of victory. From that day on, no cobra troubled Teddy's family, and Rikki-Tikki lived on in the garden, a friend of the house.

High in the hills of India, among tall trees and tumbling streams, there stood a camp of grass huts where the Government kept its working elephants and the men who drove them. The elephants hauled timber, carried loads and helped to catch their wild cousins, and the drivers had served them, father after son, for generations. Among the huts and the great grey backs, a small boy was growing up.

The boy's name was Little Toomai, and he was ten years old, the son of Big Toomai and the grandson of a driver who had served under the same flag before him. In his family there had never been a man who did not know elephants, and Little Toomai could not remember a time when he had not wished to be one. His great hope, and the dearest wish of his heart, was to be as good a driver as his father.

Big Toomai's elephant was Kala Nag, whose name means the Black Snake, a huge old working elephant with long, yellowed tusks and a skin as wrinkled as old leather. He had served the Government for many years, dragging guns through the hills and timber out of the forest, and he knew more about elephant work than most of the men who gave him orders. He was calm, wise and very proud, with a dignity that no driver in the camp could match.

Every morning at sunrise Little Toomai led Kala Nag to the river and scrubbed his rough hide with a smooth stone while the huge animal lay half in the water with an expression of deep contentment. Afterward the boy fed him sugar-cane, which the old elephant took delicately with the tip of his trunk, and lifted him up to his neck as lightly as a mother lifts a baby. It seemed to the boy that there was no better friend in the world.

The elephants of the camp stood in long lines under the trees, each with a rope around one great foot, fanning themselves with their ears and swaying gently from side to side. Pudmini, a gentle she-elephant, stood beside Kala Nag, and every one of them knew Little Toomai by sight, by smell and by the soft tone of his voice. Not one of them would have harmed him for a mountain of sugar-cane or all the gold in the Government's treasury.

Every season the men of the camp caught wild elephants by driving whole herds, step by step, into a vast stockade of tree trunks that was called the Keddah. The tame elephants went in among the wild ones to calm and control them, and it was dangerous work, for a frightened elephant can kill a man in a moment. It called for great skill and nerve, and Kala Nag had done it more times than anyone could count.

Little Toomai begged his father day after day to be allowed to go with the men to the Keddah and sit on Kala Nag's neck among the wild herds. Big Toomai, who had seen a good deal of what a frightened elephant could do, only shook his head, and said that a boy of ten must wait, and that his time would come. The boy swallowed his disappointment, and stood stubbornly silent beside the great grey elephant.

One morning Petersen Sahib, the white officer who was responsible for all the elephant catching in those hills, walked slowly along the lines, inspecting every animal with a practised eye. When he came to Kala Nag, he found the old elephant standing as quiet as a rock, with Little Toomai at his side, and he stopped and looked at the boy for a long time. Machua Appa, the chief of the drivers, stood a respectful step behind him, with folded arms.

Machua Appa told the officer that the boy was begging to be allowed into the Keddah, and Petersen Sahib, who found the idea amusing, laughed in a kindly way. He said that Little Toomai might become a catcher when he had seen the elephants dance, and everyone near by smiled. The wild elephants' dance was only a hunters' tale and a joke among the drivers, but the boy took the words seriously and never forgot them.

Little Toomai asked the old drivers, one after another, where the wild elephants danced and how a boy might find the place, and the whole camp laughed at him. They told him that nobody had ever seen such a thing, that it was a story for the evening fire and a tale for the long dark nights, and that he would do better to look to his own work. But the boy asked again, and the more he asked, the more it seemed to him that someone ought to know.

That evening the drivers sat in a ring around the camp fire and ate their rice from leaves, while the great elephants dozed in the dark behind them and swayed gently from side to side. The talk was slow and easy, as it always is after a hard day, and Little Toomai sat close to his father with his knees drawn up under his chin. He had learned that the best tales were told by men who thought that nobody was listening.

An old driver with a white beard began to speak of the dance of the wild elephants, the oldest secret of the deep jungle, and the other men fell silent as they listened. He said that on certain nights, when the moon was bright and the forest was still, the great herds slipped away from their feeding grounds and met in a hidden place to dance together. He had never seen it himself, but his father had heard of it from his own father.

He said that the dancing ground was a bare, round clearing on the top of a hill, and that the earth there had been trodden as hard as a threshing floor by the feet of many generations of elephants. No tree grew there, no grass could take root, and nobody could say how many hundreds of years the dance had been going on. The younger men glanced at one another and smiled, for they thought that the old man was telling his tale again.

Big Toomai laughed aloud, and said that the old man had told the tale a hundred times, and that no living person had ever seen the dance for himself. It was a story for children and for old men, he said, and the wise driver left it where he found it, among the dreams of the long nights. Little Toomai did not laugh, for he was thinking of Petersen Sahib's words and of the elephants' strange dance.

Later the boy crept off to Kala Nag's place at the end of the line, lay down on a heap of straw beside the great elephant and pulled his thin blanket up to his chin. One by one the fires died, the men went to their huts, and the camp grew still, so that Little Toomai could hear the leaves rustling in the dark overhead. Between the branches the stars burned small and bright, and the boy fell asleep watching them, as every child does.

Kala Nag did not settle down for the night, as he did on every other night of the year, but stood with his head high and his huge ears spread wide like two grey sails. His trunk moved restlessly from side to side, tasting the air, and now and then a deep rumble came from somewhere in his great chest. Little Toomai, who was half asleep, wondered what the old elephant could have heard in the dark.

From somewhere very far away in the hills came a sound so faint that it might have been the beating of his own heart, a low, slow thudding, like the stamp of many great feet upon the hard earth. Little Toomai sat up on his straw and held his breath, and the whole length of the elephant lines, one by one, the animals began to stir. Kala Nag answered the far-off call with a short, quiet note, and the boy felt the sound shake his ribs.

Kala Nag leaned back against the heavy chain that tied him to the picket peg, and pulled once, twice, and a third time with all his enormous weight. The stake came out of the earth with a sound like a pulled tooth, and for a moment he stood free, with the broken chain hanging from one foot. He rolled his small eyes toward the dark hills, and not a single driver in the whole camp stirred in his sleep.

Little Toomai sprang to his feet, caught hold of Kala Nag's ear and scrambled up the great shoulder onto his neck before he had a moment to be afraid. He knew, with a certainty that he could not explain, that the old elephant was going to the hills, and that wherever he went, a boy of the elephant lines must go with him. He patted the wrinkled skin with a trembling hand and whispered that he was ready.

Kala Nag turned and walked out of the sleeping camp with the boy upon his neck, and his enormous feet made no more noise on the ground than a breeze makes in the grass. Not one driver heard them go, not one dog barked, and in a few moments the dark trees had closed around the elephant like water around a stone. Ahead of them lay the hills, the moon and a secret that no man had ever seen.

Kala Nag climbed steadily through the black forest, pushing aside the hanging creepers and low branches with a sweep of his trunk, and never once did he hesitate or lose his way. Little Toomai lay flat against his neck with his arms around the thick skin, and he could feel the great muscles shifting like boulders beneath him. The night was full of the smells of wet leaves, earth and hidden water.

After a time a second elephant stepped out of the black shadows, a tall wild tusker with a rough, dusty hide and tusks that gleamed like polished bone in the moonlight. He fell in beside Kala Nag without a sound, as though he had been waiting for him, and a third came out of the trees not long afterward. Little Toomai held his breath, for he had never been so close to a wild elephant.

More and more elephants came out of the jungle on every side, tusked bulls and long-lashed cows, small calves that trotted beside their mothers and old grandfathers with sagging skin and dim, wise eyes. Before long Little Toomai was riding in the very middle of a moving river of grey backs, and the ground shook under the tramp of their enormous feet. He could not count them, and he did not try, for the whole forest seemed to be moving with the herd.

At last the long procession climbed the final slope of the hill and came out of the trees into the full silver light of the moon, and the boy found himself looking down upon a great round clearing. Not a blade of grass grew on it, not a single bush, and the earth was so hard and smooth that it rang under the elephants' feet like the floor of a threshing yard. It was the very place of which the old driver had spoken, and the boy's heart beat hard against his ribs.

Elephants poured into the clearing from every side until there were more of them than the boy had ever imagined in one place, wild ones and a few tame ones who had slipped away from their lines. The old elephant took his place among them without any fuss, as one who had been expected, and Little Toomai sat very still on his neck, hoping that nobody would notice him. A great hush fell over the hilltop, and the moon seemed to shine more brightly upon the waiting animals.

Then, without any signal that the boy could see, the dance began, slowly at first, with the great animals rocking from side to side and lifting their enormous feet in time with one another. The earth boomed beneath them like a giant drum, and the sound rolled out over the hills and valleys, carried far on the still night air. It was the sound that Kala Nag had heard from the camp, and now it was all around the boy.

The elephants circled and stamped, circled and stamped, with the white dust rising in drifting clouds around their knees and their tusks flashing like swords in the moonlight. Little Toomai felt the drumming in his bones, in his teeth and in the very roots of his hair, and he held to the old elephant's neck with all his strength. He had never seen anything so terrible and so wonderful in his whole life.

The hours went by in a haze of dust and thunder, until the moon sank low behind the trees and the first grey light crept into the eastern sky. At last the stamping grew slower and softer, and one by one the great animals drew apart, until the clearing was quiet and the dancers stood still. Little Toomai, who had ridden through the whole night, was too tired to feel afraid.

With the sunrise the herd drifted away into the jungle as quietly as it had come, and the clearing lay empty under the pale sky. Kala Nag turned for home, carrying Little Toomai, who had fallen asleep with his cheek against the warm hide, and he walked back through the waking forest to the camp. There he stopped in his old place at the picket, without a sound, as if nothing had happened.

The drivers, who had searched half the night for the missing boy, followed the broad trail up to the hilltop and found the dancing ground just as he had described it. Petersen Sahib, who had heard the tale from Machua Appa, said that Little Toomai had seen what no hunter had ever seen, and named him Toomai of the Elephants before the whole camp. A great cheer rose from the drivers, and the boy, who had gone to bed a child, felt like a king.

Mowgli walked across the hills all through the dawn, keeping his eyes on the thin smoke of the village fires that rose straight up into the windless sky. He had been born among men, but he had never lived among them, and his heart beat unevenly, as it had done on the night of the Red Flower. He wondered whether the people would feel as strange to him as he must seem to them.

When Mowgli came to the edge of the village, the people ran out of their mud houses and gathered around him in a murmuring ring, pointing and staring at the barefoot stranger. He had long black hair that fell about his shoulders, a body as brown and lean as a young wolf's, and he did not understand one word of what they said to him. The old women hid their children behind their skirts, and the dogs began to bark all along the street.

Then a thin woman called Messua came out of her hut at the far end of the street, and when she looked closely into the boy's face, she gave a low cry and put both hands to her mouth. It reminded her, she said, of her own little son Nathoo, who had been carried off by a tiger from the edge of the fields many years before. The people fell silent when they heard it, for everyone in the village knew the story of her sorrow.

Messua said that the poor child must be starving, and she took him by the hand into her small, dark house and set milk and bread before him. Mowgli could not understand her words, but a wolf-bred boy can read a face as well as a trail, and he saw that this woman wished him no harm. He ate and drank in a silence that she took for hunger and that was really wonder.

That night Mowgli lay down on the mud floor of Messua's house, and the low roof and the close walls pressed upon him until he could hardly breathe, for he had slept all his life beneath the open sky. He felt like a wild animal shut into a trap, and at last, when the house was quiet, he crept to the doorway, lay down with his face to the stars and slept. He ate and drank in a silence that she took for hunger and that was really only wonder.

Day after day Messua pointed at the objects around her, the pots and the lamps, the bread and the water, and said their names aloud, and the boy repeated each word until he had it by heart. He learned quickly, for he had already mastered the tongue of the wolves, the bears and the kites, and one more language was no great task to a boy who had learned the Master-Words. In a month, he could speak a little, and in two months he could speak freely.

The village boys laughed at the strange way that Mowgli walked and ate and sat, for he had learned no manners but a wolf's, and they made jokes that he was too proud to answer. Then they challenged him to race along the dusty lane, and he ran so lightly that he left the fastest of them far behind and was not even breathing hard when he stopped. After that day they treated him with a good deal more respect, and a few of them even asked him to teach them his running.

In the evenings the old village hunter, Buldeo, sat by the fire with his ancient gun across his knees and told the people wild tales of his adventures in the jungle, each tale larger than the last. When he spoke of a boy who had been brought up by wolves and was really a devil in the form of a child, Mowgli, who knew the truth, burst out laughing at the foolish old man. Buldeo's face grew dark with anger, and for a long time afterward the old hunter did not forgive the insult.

The headman of the village said that a boy who ate the village's bread must earn it, and he sent Mowgli out each morning to tend the buffaloes along with the other herd boys. Mowgli, to his own surprise, liked the work very much, for the huge, patient animals were easy company, and they obeyed him without argument. He sat on a broad back all day long, watching the sun cross the sky.

At the head of the herd walked Rama, the greatest bull in the district, whose broad horns swept back from his brow like the arms of a chair and whose eyes were as dark and deep as pools. He looked at Mowgli for a long, steady minute, as if taking his measure, and then he lowered his massive head and followed wherever the boy led. From that day the whole herd was Mowgli's to command, and the other boys looked at him with envy and awe.

At noon the heat of the day pressed down like a hand, and the buffaloes sank into the river until only their noses and their wide curved horns showed above the brown water. The herd boys dozed on their broad backs or splashed in the shallows, and Mowgli sat in the shade of a thorn tree and watched the river slide slowly by. It reminded him of the pools of the Seeonee hills, and of the days when he had swum there with Gray Brother.

Mowgli grew fonder of his herd with every day that passed, and he found that the great slow animals understood him when he spoke to them in low rumbling tones. He had learned many animal languages in the jungle, and the speech of the buffaloes, which was patient and plain and full of long pauses, came to him almost without effort. The calves followed him about the pasture like puppies, and Rama bowed his head when he approached.

One evening, when the sun was low and the herd was walking slowly home through the dust, a lean grey shape slipped out of the long grass at the edge of the field and stood waiting. It was Gray Brother, who had followed the village for many days at a distance, and whose flanks were thin with hunger and the weariness of a long road. Mowgli slid from the back of the buffalo and ran to him with joy.

Gray Brother told him quietly what he had seen and smelled, that Shere Khan had left his old hunting grounds and had been lying in the dry ravine beside the village for many days. The tiger knew where the herd pastured, he said, and he was waiting for the evening when the boy would be alone and far from his friends. His grey sides heaved as he spoke, and he looked at the long shadows with suspicion.

Mowgli was not afraid, and he knew the ravine well, a narrow valley with steep rocky walls and only two ways out of it, one at the top and one at the bottom. A tiger lying in its depths, he realised, would be like a fish in a stream with a net across each end, if only the two ends could be closed. He turned the thought over and over in his clever mind until it had grown into a complete and careful plan.

Mowgli told Gray Brother, in whispers, that the whole herd of buffaloes could be driven down the length of the ravine, because a tiger can face many things but cannot stand against a hundred charging bulls. He would lead the herd from the top, he said, while two wolves kept the herd in order and stopped it bursting out at the wrong end. He knew that Akela would be the best wolf for the work, and Gray Brother's eyes shone with pride and excitement at the thought.

Gray Brother turned and ran off through the thickening dusk to find Akela, who lived many miles away in the Seeonee hills and who would need all night to come. Mowgli stood watching until the grey shape had disappeared, and then he promised aloud, in the wolf's language, that he would meet them both at the head of the ravine at first light. Then he turned and drove the herd home through the dust, humming a low song to himself as he went.

That night Mowgli lay awake for a long time on the mud floor of Messua's house, listening to the slow breathing of the sleeping village and thinking of the tiger and the Pack. His heart, which had been troubled for months, was quiet at last, because he knew exactly what he meant to do and that tomorrow it would be finished. Before dawn, he rose without a sound and slipped out into the cool, dark morning.

At dawn Mowgli opened the gate of the pen and led the whole herd out into the cool grey light, and the other herd boys, who had come running with their sticks, offered to go with him. He told them lightly to stay behind, because it was his turn to take the buffaloes out alone, and they let him go with a shrug, thinking that he was a little mad. Rama walked at the head of the herd with his great horns swaying, and the earth shook gently under the weight of a hundred hooves.

At the head of the ravine, among the grey rocks and the dry bushes, Gray Brother and old Akela were waiting as they had promised, their breath white in the cool air of morning. Akela bowed his great grey head to the boy who had saved him, and Mowgli laid a hand upon it and remembered the night of the Red Flower. There was no time for long greetings, and the sun was already climbing over the edge of the hills.

Mowgli rode Rama to the very edge of the ravine and looked down into the dim, cool depths, where the rising sun had not yet reached the stones. Far below, half hidden among rocks and dry bushes, lay a long, striped shape with its great head on its paws, and there was no mistaking the tiger. Mowgli's heart beat once, hard, and then settled into a slow and steady rhythm, as it did before a hunt.

Akela and Gray Brother ran along the flank of the herd, barking and snapping, and with the skill of old shepherds they cut it cleanly in two, as though they had practised for years. One half stayed with Mowgli at the top, and the wolves drove the other half around the shoulder of the hill, out of sight, toward the lower mouth of the valley. The dust of their going hung in the cool air for a long time after the last of the wolves had vanished.

Mowgli sat quietly on Rama's broad back and waited while the wolves took their places at the far end of the valley, and the sun climbed higher, drying the dew on the grass. The bulls around him shifted and stamped and tossed their heads, as though they understood that something very large was about to happen. He had never in his life been more patient, and he did not fidget.

When the sun was well up, Mowgli cupped his hands to his mouth and called down into the ravine in the tongue of the jungle, and the echoes ran down the valley like a river. He called the tiger by his name, the Lame One, the cattle-killer, and told him that the man-cub whom he had hunted for so many years had come to meet him at last. Then he sat back on the bull's broad back and waited for an answer from the dark depths.

Shere Khan rose slowly to his feet with a snarl that shook the dust from the walls of the ravine, and he stared up at the small figure on the great bull above him. Then he turned his head and looked down the valley, where the lower end had filled with the black bodies of the other half of the herd, and for the first time in his life he understood fear. It was the cold, helpless fear of a creature that has been hunter all its life and finds that it has no way out.

Shere Khan sprang at the rocky wall of the ravine and tried to scramble up its side, but the stone was as steep and smooth as the wall of a house, and his old lame foot slipped on every ledge. Three times he flung himself at it, and three times he slid back to the bottom with his claws screeching on the rock, snarling with rage and helplessness. There was no way out above him, no way out below him, and the sun beat down on the narrow walls.

Mowgli raised his arm high above his head and gave the herd the wild cry that he had taught them, a sound halfway between a shout and a howl, which echoed across the hills. Rama lowered his enormous horns and plunged forward, and behind him, with a roar like an avalanche, the whole herd of bulls poured over the edge into the ravine. The ground shook as though the whole hill were about to split, and the sky went dark with dust.

The herd thundered down the narrow valley like a flood of horns and dust, shaking the very rocks with its fury, and the noise was so great that Mowgli could hear nothing else in all the world. At the lower end the wolves, barking like mad, drove the second half to meet them, so that the tiger was shut in between two walls of angry buffaloes with nowhere to turn. It was over almost before the boy knew that the great stampede had begun, and it left him breathless.

Shere Khan, trapped between the two halves of the herd with steep walls on either side, had no place to turn, and his long hunt for the man-cub ended there in the dust and the thunder. When the dust settled at last and the noise died away, the ravine lay silent, and the buffaloes stood shaking their heads and blowing through their noses. The old terror of the Seeonee hills was dead, and the herd had done what no wolf or bear had ever managed.

Mowgli rode down into the quiet ravine, where the herd had settled and the dust was turning slowly gold in the sunshine, and he stood beside the great striped body of his enemy. He felt no joy and no hatred, only a great quiet, as he thought of the night when he had left the Pack with tears in his eyes. He remembered the promise that he had made at Council Rock, and he knew that the time had come to keep it.

Mowgli took out the little knife that he had brought from the village and set to work upon the great striped hide, as he had seen the village men skin the deer. The work was hard and took most of the morning, and Akela and Gray Brother sat on their haunches and watched in silence, as though they were witnessing a ceremony. At last the skin lay spread upon the stones, whole and glorious in the sun.

While Mowgli was still at work, there was a clatter on the path above the ravine, and old Buldeo came puffing and wheezing down the slope with his ancient gun on his shoulder. He had come looking for the herd, which the other boys had reported missing, and he stopped dead when he saw the great skin spread out upon the stones. His small eyes grew round with greed, and he licked his lips as he looked at the beautiful skin.

Buldeo said, in a loud and pompous voice, that the tiger had been his own prey for many years, and that the skin must be handed over to him at once. He knew that the Government paid a handsome reward for every tiger killed in the district, and he meant to say that he himself had done the deed, with his old gun. Nobody in the village would have doubted a word of it, for Buldeo was known to everyone as a mighty hunter.

Mowgli answered quietly that the skin was not for sale and not for the Government, and that he had made a promise long ago that it should lie on the Council Rock of the Seeonee wolves. He told the old hunter that he had not killed the tiger for any reward, but because the tiger had hunted him since he was a baby. Buldeo stared at him as though he had gone mad, for nobody had ever before refused the Government's money.

Buldeo grew red in the face, and he raised his old gun to threaten the boy, but at that moment two grey wolves, Akela and Gray Brother, rose silently from the rocks behind him and showed all their teeth. The hunter's face went from red to white, the gun slipped from his shaking hands, and his knees knocked together as he stared at the boy and the beasts. He had heard the stories of wolf-boys all his life, and now he believed every one of them.

Buldeo turned and ran for the village as fast as his old legs would carry him, screaming that Mowgli was a sorcerer, a devil in a child's shape who spoke with wolves and commanded wild beasts. He did not stop shouting until he had reached the door of the headman's house, where a crowd was already gathering to hear his tale. By the time he had finished, the story had grown a good deal in the telling.

Mowgli sighed, for he had hoped to keep his friends and his promises both, and he rolled up the great skin, flung it over his shoulder and drove the buffaloes slowly back toward the village. The herd belonged to the villagers, and he did not wish to leave it on the hillside, where it might stray. He had no idea what Buldeo had said about him, or how quickly the tale had spread.

When Mowgli came to the edge of the fields, he saw that a crowd of angry men with sticks and axes was waiting at the gate, and that the women stood behind them with pale, frightened faces. They shouted that he was a sorcerer and a wizard, a devil in a boy's shape who spoke to wolves and had called the buffaloes against a tiger. Not one of them remembered that he had been a cheerful, helpful boy who had worked beside them for months.

Frightened and ignorant, the villagers took up the cry, shut their doors against Mowgli, and began to hurl stones as he passed, one of which struck him painfully on the shoulder. He stood quite still in the road, for he could not understand why the people whom he had served so well should suddenly throw stones at him. Then, with the stones still falling about him, he walked on down the street without lifting a hand to defend himself.

Messua stood weeping in the doorway of her house, for she had come to love the strange, silent boy, but she was only one woman against a whole angry village, and she knew that she could not help him. Mowgli looked at her kind face once, with something like sorrow, and then he turned and walked away into the dusk with the tiger's skin over his shoulder. He did not look back again, for he knew that if he did, he would not be able to go on.

Mowgli walked on across the dark fields until the first trees of the jungle rose before him like a black wall, and he stepped into their shade with the tiger's skin on his shoulder. The old night smells of damp earth, wet leaves and hidden water rose around him, and the sounds of the night birds and the little beasts of the grass seemed to speak his name. It was like being greeted by a hundred old friends at once, and for the first time in many days he smiled.

Before long Akela and Gray Brother, who had followed him from the village, came out of the shadows and ran silently at his side, and no words were needed to tell him that they were glad. The three of them went on together toward the hills of the Seeonee as the moon rose slowly through the branches, and the long road seemed to pass in a moment. Mowgli did not once look back toward the lights of the village, for his road now lay in the other direction.

At dawn they came to the old cave on the hillside where Mowgli had been raised, and Mother Wolf ran out to meet him and licked his face again and again, as if he were still a naked baby. Father Wolf stood at her shoulder with his tail swinging, trying to look dignified and failing badly, and the four tumbling cubs of long ago, now great grown wolves, came crowding round the boy. It was the happiest dawn that anyone in the cave could remember, and nobody wished it to end.

Mowgli sat at the mouth of the cave in the early sunshine and told his wolf family the whole tale, from the buffalo herd and the ravine to the tiger's fall and the angry village. Mother Wolf listened with her head on one side, and when he had finished, she said proudly that she had always known he would keep his promise to bring back the tiger's skin. Father Wolf said nothing, but his eyes shone, and when the story was done, Mowgli, who had not slept for two nights, lay down on his old bed and slept the whole day through.

When the sun went down, Mowgli woke from his long sleep, washed in the stream and walked up to the Council Rock with the rolled skin under his arm, while the whole hillside watched him in silence. He spread it flat upon the great stone, as he had promised on the night that he left, and he weighted the corners with four heavy rocks so that the evening wind could not lift it. The stripes glowed like fire in the last red light, and the wolves who had gathered below were silent.

Standing beside the skin, Mowgli threw back his head and gave the old call of the Seeonee Pack, the long, rising cry that summoned the Free People to Council, and it carried over the hills and into the valleys. The wolves came running from every direction, young and old, grey and black, and Akela, leaping onto his own stone, called out the ancient words that began every gathering: Look well, O Wolves. Soon the great rock was ringed with grey, and every face was turned toward the boy and the skin.

The wolves crowded around the Council Rock and stared at the tiger's skin as though they could scarcely believe their own eyes, and for a long moment nobody uttered a sound. Then a great cry of welcome rose from the whole Pack at once, the same wolves who had once been ready to turn on the man-cub, now shouting his name to the sky. Akela, who knew how much the boy had done for him, was the first to bow his head.

The wolves begged Mowgli to come back to the Pack and lead them in the place of the aged Akela, saying that no leader could be braver or wiser than the boy who had killed the tiger. Mowgli thanked them warmly, but he said that Akela was still their rightful chief, and that he himself would rather be their brother than their master, running at their side and sharing their hunts. A low sound of delight ran round the ring, and Akela, lying on his stone, closed his eyes with quiet satisfaction.

Mowgli stood upon the tiger's skin and sang a wild, glad song of the hunt, telling of the long years and the Red Flower and the great stampede, while Baloo and Bagheera came out of the trees. Bagheera purred that he had never doubted the boy for a moment, and old Baloo rubbed his eyes and said gruffly that the lessons had not been wasted. The wolves howled their joy until the very hills rang with it, and the sound was heard for many miles.

And so the boy who had been carried into a wolf's cave as a naked baby ran once more with the Pack through the silver forest, a creature who belonged to the jungle by choice as well as by upbringing. Shere Khan was gone, the Red Flower slept in its pot, and the Law of the Jungle held as firm as it had ever done. Over the hills the moon sailed high and white, and the whole night was full of the happy voices of Mowgli's friends.
